# pest - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/pest/latest/target-redirect/pest/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#pest-the-elegant-parser)pest. The Elegant Parser

pest is a general purpose parser written in Rust with a focus on accessibility, correctness,
and performance. It uses parsing expression grammars (or [PEG](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parsing_expression_grammar)) as input, which are similar in
spirit to regular expressions, but which offer the enhanced expressivity needed to parse
complex languages.

[§](https://docs.rs#getting-started)Getting started

The recommended way to start parsing with pest is to read the official [book](https://pest.rs/book).

Other helpful resources:

- API reference on [docs.rs](https://docs.rs/pest)
- play with grammars and share them on our [fiddle](https://pest.rs/#editor)
- find previous common questions answered or ask questions on [GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/pest-parser/pest/discussions)
- leave feedback, ask questions, or greet us on [Gitter](https://gitter.im/pest-parser/pest)or[Discord](https://discord.gg/XEGACtWpT2)

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

The core of pest is the trait [ Parser](https://docs.rs/trait.Parser.html), which provides an interface to the parsing
functionality.

The accompanying crate `pest_derive` can automatically generate a [ Parser](https://docs.rs/trait.Parser.html) from a PEG
grammar. Using

`pest_derive` is highly encouraged, but it is also possible to implement
[manually if required.](https://docs.rs/trait.Parser.html)

`Parser`[§](https://docs.rs#pest-files)`.pest` files

Grammar definitions reside in custom `.pest` files located in the crate `src` directory.
Parsers are automatically generated from these files using `#[derive(Parser)]` and a special
`#[grammar = "..."]` attribute on a dummy struct.

The syntax of `.pest` files is documented in the [ pest_derive crate](https://docs.rs/pest_derive/).

[§](https://docs.rs#inline-grammars)Inline grammars

Grammars can also be inlined by using the `#[grammar_inline = "..."]` attribute.

[§](https://docs.rs#grammar)Grammar

A grammar is a series of rules separated by whitespace, possibly containing comments.

[§](https://docs.rs#comments)Comments

Comments start with `//` and end at the end of the line.

`// a comment`[§](https://docs.rs#rules)Rules

Rules have the following form:

The name of the rule is formed from alphanumeric characters or `_` with the condition that the
first character is not a digit and is used to create token pairs. When the rule starts being
parsed, the starting part of the token is being produced, with the ending part being produced
when the rule finishes parsing.

The following token pair notation `a(b(), c())` denotes the tokens: start `a`, start `b`, end
`b`, start `c`, end `c`, end `a`.

[§](https://docs.rs#modifiers)Modifiers

Modifiers are optional and can be one of `_`, `@`, `$`, or `!`. These modifiers change the
behavior of the rules.

-
Silent ( `_`)Silent rules do not create token pairs during parsing, nor are they error-reported. Parsing `"ab"`produces the token pair`b()`.
-
Atomic ( `@`)Atomic rules do not accept whitespace or comments within their expressions and have a cascading effect on any rule they call. I.e. rules that are not atomic but are called by atomic rules behave atomically. Any rules called by atomic rules do not generate token pairs. Parsing `"ab"`produces the token pair`b()`, while`"a b"`produces an error.
-
Compound-atomic ( `$`)Compound-atomic are identical to atomic rules with the exception that rules called by them are not forbidden from generating token pairs. Parsing `"ab"`produces the token pairs`b(a())`, while`"a b"`produces an error.
-
Non-atomic ( `!`)Non-atomic are identical to normal rules with the exception that they stop the cascading effect of atomic and compound-atomic rules. Parsing both `"ab"`and`"a b"`produce the token pairs`c(a())`.

[§](https://docs.rs#expressions)Expressions

Expressions can be either terminals or non-terminals.

- Terminals

| Terminal | Usage |
|---|---|
| `"a"` | matches the exact string `"a"` |
| `^"a"` | matches the exact string `"a"`case insensitively (ASCII only) |
| `'a'..'z'` | matches one character between `'a'`and`'z'` |
| `a` | matches rule `a` |

Strings and characters follow
[Rust’s escape mechanisms](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/tokens.html#byte-escapes), while
identifiers can contain alphanumeric characters and underscores (`_`), as long as they do not
start with a digit.

- Non-terminals

| Non-terminal | Usage |
|---|---|
| `(e)` | matches `e` |
| `e1 ~ e2` | matches the sequence `e1``e2` |
| `e1 | e2` | matches either `e1`or`e2` |
| `e*` | matches `e`zero or more times |
| `e+` | matches `e`one or more times |
| `e{n}` | matches `e`exactly`n`times |
| `e{, n}` | matches `e`at most`n`times |
| `e{n,}` | matches `e`at least`n`times |
| `e{m, n}` | matches `e`between`m`and`n`times inclusively |
| `e?` | optionally matches `e` |
| `&e` | matches `e`without making progress |
| `!e` | matches if `e`doesn’t match without making progress |
| `PUSH(e)` | matches `e`and pushes it’s captured string down the stack |

where `e`, `e1`, and `e2` are expressions.

Matching is greedy, without backtracking. Note the difference in behavior for these two rules in matching identifiers that don’t end in an underscore:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
// input: ab_bb_b
identifier = @{ "a" ~ ("b"|"_")* ~ "b" }
// matches:      a     b_bb_b       nothing -> error!
identifier = @{ "a" ~ ("_"* ~ "b")* }
// matches:      a     b, _bb, _b   in three repetitions
```
Expressions can modify the stack only if they match the input. For example,
if `e1` in the compound expression `e1 | e2` does not match the input, then
it does not modify the stack, so `e2` sees the stack in the same state as
`e1` did. Repetitions and optionals (`e*`, `e+`, `e{, n}`, `e{n,}`,
`e{m,n}`, `e?`) can modify the stack each time `e` matches. The `!e` and `&e`
expressions are a special case; they never modify the stack.
Many languages have “keyword” tokens (e.g. if, for, while) as well as general
tokens (e.g. identifier) that matches any word. In order to match a keyword,
generally, you may need to restrict that is not immediately followed by another
letter or digit (otherwise it would be matched as an identifier).

[§](https://docs.rs#special-rules)Special rules

Special rules can be called within the grammar. They are:

- `WHITESPACE`- runs between rules and sub-rules
- `COMMENT`- runs between rules and sub-rules
- `ANY`- matches exactly one- `char`
- `SOI`- (start-of-input) matches only when a- `Parser`is still at the starting position
- `EOI`- (end-of-input) matches only when a- `Parser`has reached its end
- `PUSH`- matches a string and pushes it to the stack
- `PUSH_LITERAL`- pushes a literal string to the stack
- `POP`- pops a string from the stack and matches it
- `POP_ALL`- pops the entire state of the stack and matches it
- `PEEK`- peeks a string from the stack and matches it
- `PEEK[a..b]`- peeks part of the stack and matches it
- `PEEK_ALL`- peeks the entire state of the stack and matches it
- `DROP`- drops the top of the stack (fails to match if the stack is empty)

`WHITESPACE` and `COMMENT` should be defined manually if needed. All other rules cannot be
overridden.

[§](https://docs.rs#whitespace-and-comment)`WHITESPACE` and `COMMENT`

When defined, these rules get matched automatically in sequences (`~`) and repetitions
(`*`, `+`) between expressions. Atomic rules and those rules called by atomic rules are exempt
from this behavior.

These rules should be defined so as to match one whitespace character and one comment only since they are run in repetitions.

If both `WHITESPACE` and `COMMENT` are defined, this grammar:

is effectively transformed into this one behind the scenes:

[§](https://docs.rs#push-push_literal-pop-drop-and-peek)`PUSH`, `PUSH_LITERAL`, `POP`, `DROP`, and `PEEK`

`PUSH(e)` simply pushes the captured string of the expression `e` down a stack. This stack can
then later be used to match grammar based on its content with `POP` and `PEEK`.

`PUSH_LITERAL("a")` pushes the argument to the stack without considering the input. The
argument must be a literal string. This is often useful in conjunction with another rule before
it. For example, `"[" ~ PUSH_LITERAL("]")` will look for an opening bracket `[` and, if it
finds one, will push a closing bracket `]` to the stack. **Note**: `PUSH_LITERAL` requires the
`grammar-extras` feature to be enabled.

`PEEK` always matches the string at the top of stack. So, if the stack contains `["b", "a"]`
(`"a"` being on top), this grammar:

is effectively transformed into at parse time:

`POP` works the same way with the exception that it pops the string off of the stack if the
match worked. With the stack from above, if `POP` matches `"a"`, the stack will be mutated
to `["b"]`.

`DROP` makes it possible to remove the string at the top of the stack
without matching it. If the stack is nonempty, `DROP` drops the top of the
stack. If the stack is empty, then `DROP` fails to match.

[§](https://docs.rs#advanced-peeking)Advanced peeking

`PEEK[start..end]` and `PEEK_ALL` allow to peek deeper into the stack. The syntax works exactly
like Rust’s exclusive slice syntax. Additionally, negative indices can be used to indicate an
offset from the top. If the end lies before or at the start, the expression matches (as does
a `PEEK_ALL` on an empty stack). With the stack `["c", "b", "a"]` (`"a"` on top):

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
fill = PUSH("c") ~ PUSH("b") ~ PUSH("a")
v = { PEEK_ALL } = { "a" ~ "b" ~ "c" }  // top to bottom
w = { PEEK[..] } = { "c" ~ "b" ~ "a" }  // bottom to top
x = { PEEK[1..2] } = { PEEK[1..-1] } = { "b" }
y = { PEEK[..-2] } = { PEEK[0..1] } = { "a" }
z = { PEEK[1..] } = { PEEK[-2..3] } = { "c" ~ "b" }
n = { PEEK[2..-2] } = { PEEK[2..1] } = { "" }
```
For historical reasons, `PEEK_ALL` matches from top to bottom, while `PEEK[start..end]` matches
from bottom to top. There is currently no syntax to match a slice of the stack top to bottom.

[§](https://docs.rs#rule)`Rule`

All rules defined or used in the grammar populate a generated `enum` called `Rule`. This
implements `pest`’s `RuleType` and can be used throughout the API.

[§](https://docs.rs#built-in-rules)`Built-in rules`

Pest also comes with a number of built-in rules for convenience. They are:

- `ASCII_DIGIT`- matches a numeric character from 0..9
- `ASCII_NONZERO_DIGIT`- matches a numeric character from 1..9
- `ASCII_BIN_DIGIT`- matches a numeric character from 0..1
- `ASCII_OCT_DIGIT`- matches a numeric character from 0..7
- `ASCII_HEX_DIGIT`- matches a numeric character from 0..9 or a..f or A..F
- `ASCII_ALPHA_LOWER`- matches a character from a..z
- `ASCII_ALPHA_UPPER`- matches a character from A..Z
- `ASCII_ALPHA`- matches a character from a..z or A..Z
- `ASCII_ALPHANUMERIC`- matches a character from a..z or A..Z or 0..9
- `ASCII`- matches a character from \x00..\x7f
- `NEWLINE`- matches either “\n” or “\r\n” or “\r”

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [error](https://docs.rs/error/index.html)
- Types for different kinds of parsing failures.
- [iterators](https://docs.rs/iterators/index.html)
- Types and iterators for parser output.
- [pratt_](https://docs.rs/pratt_parser/index.html)- parser
- Constructs useful in prefix, postfix, and infix operator parsing with the Pratt parsing method.
- [prec_](https://docs.rs/prec_climber/index.html)- climber - Deprecated
- Constructs useful in infix operator parsing with the precedence climbing method.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [fails_](https://docs.rs/macro.fails_with.html)- with
- Testing tool that compares produced errors.
- [parses_](https://docs.rs/macro.parses_to.html)- to
- Testing tool that compares produced tokens.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Lines](https://docs.rs/struct.Lines.html)
- Line iterator for Spans, created by `Span::lines()`
- [Lines](https://docs.rs/struct.LinesSpan.html)- Span
- Line iterator for Spans, created by `Span::lines_span()`
- [Parser](https://docs.rs/struct.ParserState.html)- State
- The complete state of a `Parser`
- [Position](https://docs.rs/struct.Position.html)
- A cursor position in a `&str`which provides useful methods to manually parse that string.
- [Span](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html)
- A span over a `&str`. It is created from either[two](https://docs.rs/struct.Position.html#method.span)or from a`Position`s`Pair`
- [Stack](https://docs.rs/struct.Stack.html)
- Implementation of a `Stack`which maintains popped elements and length of previous states in order to rewind the stack to a previous state.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Atomicity](https://docs.rs/enum.Atomicity.html)
- The current atomicity of a `ParserState`
- [Lookahead](https://docs.rs/enum.Lookahead.html)
- The current lookahead status of a `ParserState`
- [Match](https://docs.rs/enum.MatchDir.html)- Dir
- Match direction for the stack. Used in `PEEK[a..b]`/`stack_match_peek_slice`.
- [Token](https://docs.rs/enum.Token.html)
- A token generated by a `Parser`.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Parser](https://docs.rs/trait.Parser.html)
- A trait with a single method that parses strings.
- [Rule](https://docs.rs/trait.RuleType.html)- Type
- A trait which parser rules must implement.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [merge_](https://docs.rs/fn.merge_spans.html)- spans
- Merges two spans into one.
- [set_](https://docs.rs/fn.set_call_limit.html)- call_ - limit
- Sets the maximum call limit for the parser state to prevent stack overflows or excessive execution times in some grammars. If set, the calls are tracked as a running total over all non-terminal rules that can nest closures (which are passed to transform the parser state).
- [set_](https://docs.rs/fn.set_error_detail.html)- error_ - detail
- Sets whether information for more error details should be collected. This is useful for debugging parser errors (as it leads to more comprehensive error messages), but it has a higher performance cost. (hence, it’s off by default)
- [state](https://docs.rs/fn.state.html)
- Creates a `ParserState`from a`&str`, supplying it to a closure`f`.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Parse](https://docs.rs/type.ParseResult.html)- Result
- Type alias to simplify specifying the return value of chained closures.

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

---

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (4c9d2bfe4 2026-07-01)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

# pest - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/pest

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#pest-the-elegant-parser)pest. The Elegant Parser

pest is a general purpose parser written in Rust with a focus on accessibility, correctness,
and performance. It uses parsing expression grammars (or [PEG](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parsing_expression_grammar)) as input, which are similar in
spirit to regular expressions, but which offer the enhanced expressivity needed to parse
complex languages.

[§](https://docs.rs#getting-started)Getting started

The recommended way to start parsing with pest is to read the official [book](https://pest.rs/book).

Other helpful resources:

- API reference on [docs.rs](https://docs.rs/pest)
- play with grammars and share them on our [fiddle](https://pest.rs/#editor)
- find previous common questions answered or ask questions on [GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/pest-parser/pest/discussions)
- leave feedback, ask questions, or greet us on [Gitter](https://gitter.im/pest-parser/pest)or[Discord](https://discord.gg/XEGACtWpT2)

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

The core of pest is the trait [ Parser](https://docs.rs/trait.Parser.html), which provides an interface to the parsing
functionality.

The accompanying crate `pest_derive` can automatically generate a [ Parser](https://docs.rs/trait.Parser.html) from a PEG
grammar. Using

`pest_derive` is highly encouraged, but it is also possible to implement
[manually if required.](https://docs.rs/trait.Parser.html)

`Parser`[§](https://docs.rs#pest-files)`.pest` files

Grammar definitions reside in custom `.pest` files located in the crate `src` directory.
Parsers are automatically generated from these files using `#[derive(Parser)]` and a special
`#[grammar = "..."]` attribute on a dummy struct.

The syntax of `.pest` files is documented in the [ pest_derive crate](https://docs.rs/pest_derive/).

[§](https://docs.rs#inline-grammars)Inline grammars

Grammars can also be inlined by using the `#[grammar_inline = "..."]` attribute.

[§](https://docs.rs#grammar)Grammar

A grammar is a series of rules separated by whitespace, possibly containing comments.

[§](https://docs.rs#comments)Comments

Comments start with `//` and end at the end of the line.

`// a comment`[§](https://docs.rs#rules)Rules

Rules have the following form:

The name of the rule is formed from alphanumeric characters or `_` with the condition that the
first character is not a digit and is used to create token pairs. When the rule starts being
parsed, the starting part of the token is being produced, with the ending part being produced
when the rule finishes parsing.

The following token pair notation `a(b(), c())` denotes the tokens: start `a`, start `b`, end
`b`, start `c`, end `c`, end `a`.

[§](https://docs.rs#modifiers)Modifiers

Modifiers are optional and can be one of `_`, `@`, `$`, or `!`. These modifiers change the
behavior of the rules.

-
Silent ( `_`)Silent rules do not create token pairs during parsing, nor are they error-reported. Parsing `"ab"`produces the token pair`b()`.
-
Atomic ( `@`)Atomic rules do not accept whitespace or comments within their expressions and have a cascading effect on any rule they call. I.e. rules that are not atomic but are called by atomic rules behave atomically. Any rules called by atomic rules do not generate token pairs. Parsing `"ab"`produces the token pair`b()`, while`"a b"`produces an error.
-
Compound-atomic ( `$`)Compound-atomic are identical to atomic rules with the exception that rules called by them are not forbidden from generating token pairs. Parsing `"ab"`produces the token pairs`b(a())`, while`"a b"`produces an error.
-
Non-atomic ( `!`)Non-atomic are identical to normal rules with the exception that they stop the cascading effect of atomic and compound-atomic rules. Parsing both `"ab"`and`"a b"`produce the token pairs`c(a())`.

[§](https://docs.rs#expressions)Expressions

Expressions can be either terminals or non-terminals.

- Terminals

| Terminal | Usage |
|---|---|
| `"a"` | matches the exact string `"a"` |
| `^"a"` | matches the exact string `"a"`case insensitively (ASCII only) |
| `'a'..'z'` | matches one character between `'a'`and`'z'` |
| `a` | matches rule `a` |

Strings and characters follow
[Rust’s escape mechanisms](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/tokens.html#byte-escapes), while
identifiers can contain alphanumeric characters and underscores (`_`), as long as they do not
start with a digit.

- Non-terminals

| Non-terminal | Usage |
|---|---|
| `(e)` | matches `e` |
| `e1 ~ e2` | matches the sequence `e1``e2` |
| `e1 | e2` | matches either `e1`or`e2` |
| `e*` | matches `e`zero or more times |
| `e+` | matches `e`one or more times |
| `e{n}` | matches `e`exactly`n`times |
| `e{, n}` | matches `e`at most`n`times |
| `e{n,}` | matches `e`at least`n`times |
| `e{m, n}` | matches `e`between`m`and`n`times inclusively |
| `e?` | optionally matches `e` |
| `&e` | matches `e`without making progress |
| `!e` | matches if `e`doesn’t match without making progress |
| `PUSH(e)` | matches `e`and pushes it’s captured string down the stack |

where `e`, `e1`, and `e2` are expressions.

Matching is greedy, without backtracking. Note the difference in behavior for these two rules in matching identifiers that don’t end in an underscore:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
// input: ab_bb_b
identifier = @{ "a" ~ ("b"|"_")* ~ "b" }
// matches:      a     b_bb_b       nothing -> error!
identifier = @{ "a" ~ ("_"* ~ "b")* }
// matches:      a     b, _bb, _b   in three repetitions
```
Expressions can modify the stack only if they match the input. For example,
if `e1` in the compound expression `e1 | e2` does not match the input, then
it does not modify the stack, so `e2` sees the stack in the same state as
`e1` did. Repetitions and optionals (`e*`, `e+`, `e{, n}`, `e{n,}`,
`e{m,n}`, `e?`) can modify the stack each time `e` matches. The `!e` and `&e`
expressions are a special case; they never modify the stack.
Many languages have “keyword” tokens (e.g. if, for, while) as well as general
tokens (e.g. identifier) that matches any word. In order to match a keyword,
generally, you may need to restrict that is not immediately followed by another
letter or digit (otherwise it would be matched as an identifier).

[§](https://docs.rs#special-rules)Special rules

Special rules can be called within the grammar. They are:

- `WHITESPACE`- runs between rules and sub-rules
- `COMMENT`- runs between rules and sub-rules
- `ANY`- matches exactly one- `char`
- `SOI`- (start-of-input) matches only when a- `Parser`is still at the starting position
- `EOI`- (end-of-input) matches only when a- `Parser`has reached its end
- `PUSH`- matches a string and pushes it to the stack
- `PUSH_LITERAL`- pushes a literal string to the stack
- `POP`- pops a string from the stack and matches it
- `POP_ALL`- pops the entire state of the stack and matches it
- `PEEK`- peeks a string from the stack and matches it
- `PEEK[a..b]`- peeks part of the stack and matches it
- `PEEK_ALL`- peeks the entire state of the stack and matches it
- `DROP`- drops the top of the stack (fails to match if the stack is empty)

`WHITESPACE` and `COMMENT` should be defined manually if needed. All other rules cannot be
overridden.

[§](https://docs.rs#whitespace-and-comment)`WHITESPACE` and `COMMENT`

When defined, these rules get matched automatically in sequences (`~`) and repetitions
(`*`, `+`) between expressions. Atomic rules and those rules called by atomic rules are exempt
from this behavior.

These rules should be defined so as to match one whitespace character and one comment only since they are run in repetitions.

If both `WHITESPACE` and `COMMENT` are defined, this grammar:

is effectively transformed into this one behind the scenes:

[§](https://docs.rs#push-push_literal-pop-drop-and-peek)`PUSH`, `PUSH_LITERAL`, `POP`, `DROP`, and `PEEK`

`PUSH(e)` simply pushes the captured string of the expression `e` down a stack. This stack can
then later be used to match grammar based on its content with `POP` and `PEEK`.

`PUSH_LITERAL("a")` pushes the argument to the stack without considering the input. The
argument must be a literal string. This is often useful in conjunction with another rule before
it. For example, `"[" ~ PUSH_LITERAL("]")` will look for an opening bracket `[` and, if it
finds one, will push a closing bracket `]` to the stack. **Note**: `PUSH_LITERAL` requires the
`grammar-extras` feature to be enabled.

`PEEK` always matches the string at the top of stack. So, if the stack contains `["b", "a"]`
(`"a"` being on top), this grammar:

is effectively transformed into at parse time:

`POP` works the same way with the exception that it pops the string off of the stack if the
match worked. With the stack from above, if `POP` matches `"a"`, the stack will be mutated
to `["b"]`.

`DROP` makes it possible to remove the string at the top of the stack
without matching it. If the stack is nonempty, `DROP` drops the top of the
stack. If the stack is empty, then `DROP` fails to match.

[§](https://docs.rs#advanced-peeking)Advanced peeking

`PEEK[start..end]` and `PEEK_ALL` allow to peek deeper into the stack. The syntax works exactly
like Rust’s exclusive slice syntax. Additionally, negative indices can be used to indicate an
offset from the top. If the end lies before or at the start, the expression matches (as does
a `PEEK_ALL` on an empty stack). With the stack `["c", "b", "a"]` (`"a"` on top):

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
fill = PUSH("c") ~ PUSH("b") ~ PUSH("a")
v = { PEEK_ALL } = { "a" ~ "b" ~ "c" }  // top to bottom
w = { PEEK[..] } = { "c" ~ "b" ~ "a" }  // bottom to top
x = { PEEK[1..2] } = { PEEK[1..-1] } = { "b" }
y = { PEEK[..-2] } = { PEEK[0..1] } = { "a" }
z = { PEEK[1..] } = { PEEK[-2..3] } = { "c" ~ "b" }
n = { PEEK[2..-2] } = { PEEK[2..1] } = { "" }
```
For historical reasons, `PEEK_ALL` matches from top to bottom, while `PEEK[start..end]` matches
from bottom to top. There is currently no syntax to match a slice of the stack top to bottom.

[§](https://docs.rs#rule)`Rule`

All rules defined or used in the grammar populate a generated `enum` called `Rule`. This
implements `pest`’s `RuleType` and can be used throughout the API.

[§](https://docs.rs#built-in-rules)`Built-in rules`

Pest also comes with a number of built-in rules for convenience. They are:

- `ASCII_DIGIT`- matches a numeric character from 0..9
- `ASCII_NONZERO_DIGIT`- matches a numeric character from 1..9
- `ASCII_BIN_DIGIT`- matches a numeric character from 0..1
- `ASCII_OCT_DIGIT`- matches a numeric character from 0..7
- `ASCII_HEX_DIGIT`- matches a numeric character from 0..9 or a..f or A..F
- `ASCII_ALPHA_LOWER`- matches a character from a..z
- `ASCII_ALPHA_UPPER`- matches a character from A..Z
- `ASCII_ALPHA`- matches a character from a..z or A..Z
- `ASCII_ALPHANUMERIC`- matches a character from a..z or A..Z or 0..9
- `ASCII`- matches a character from \x00..\x7f
- `NEWLINE`- matches either “\n” or “\r\n” or “\r”

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [error](https://docs.rs/error/index.html)
- Types for different kinds of parsing failures.
- [iterators](https://docs.rs/iterators/index.html)
- Types and iterators for parser output.
- [pratt_](https://docs.rs/pratt_parser/index.html)- parser
- Constructs useful in prefix, postfix, and infix operator parsing with the Pratt parsing method.
- [prec_](https://docs.rs/prec_climber/index.html)- climber - Deprecated
- Constructs useful in infix operator parsing with the precedence climbing method.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [fails_](https://docs.rs/macro.fails_with.html)- with
- Testing tool that compares produced errors.
- [parses_](https://docs.rs/macro.parses_to.html)- to
- Testing tool that compares produced tokens.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Lines](https://docs.rs/struct.Lines.html)
- Line iterator for Spans, created by `Span::lines()`
- [Lines](https://docs.rs/struct.LinesSpan.html)- Span
- Line iterator for Spans, created by `Span::lines_span()`
- [Parser](https://docs.rs/struct.ParserState.html)- State
- The complete state of a `Parser`
- [Position](https://docs.rs/struct.Position.html)
- A cursor position in a `&str`which provides useful methods to manually parse that string.
- [Span](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html)
- A span over a `&str`. It is created from either[two](https://docs.rs/struct.Position.html#method.span)or from a`Position`s`Pair`
- [Stack](https://docs.rs/struct.Stack.html)
- Implementation of a `Stack`which maintains popped elements and length of previous states in order to rewind the stack to a previous state.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Atomicity](https://docs.rs/enum.Atomicity.html)
- The current atomicity of a `ParserState`
- [Lookahead](https://docs.rs/enum.Lookahead.html)
- The current lookahead status of a `ParserState`
- [Match](https://docs.rs/enum.MatchDir.html)- Dir
- Match direction for the stack. Used in `PEEK[a..b]`/`stack_match_peek_slice`.
- [Token](https://docs.rs/enum.Token.html)
- A token generated by a `Parser`.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Parser](https://docs.rs/trait.Parser.html)
- A trait with a single method that parses strings.
- [Rule](https://docs.rs/trait.RuleType.html)- Type
- A trait which parser rules must implement.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [merge_](https://docs.rs/fn.merge_spans.html)- spans
- Merges two spans into one.
- [set_](https://docs.rs/fn.set_call_limit.html)- call_ - limit
- Sets the maximum call limit for the parser state to prevent stack overflows or excessive execution times in some grammars. If set, the calls are tracked as a running total over all non-terminal rules that can nest closures (which are passed to transform the parser state).
- [set_](https://docs.rs/fn.set_error_detail.html)- error_ - detail
- Sets whether information for more error details should be collected. This is useful for debugging parser errors (as it leads to more comprehensive error messages), but it has a higher performance cost. (hence, it’s off by default)
- [state](https://docs.rs/fn.state.html)
- Creates a `ParserState`from a`&str`, supplying it to a closure`f`.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Parse](https://docs.rs/type.ParseResult.html)- Result
- Type alias to simplify specifying the return value of chained closures.

# pest_derive - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/pest_derive/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#pest-the-elegant-parser)pest. The Elegant Parser

pest is a general purpose parser written in Rust with a focus on accessibility, correctness,
and performance. It uses parsing expression grammars (or [PEG](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parsing_expression_grammar)) as input, which are similar in
spirit to regular expressions, but which offer the enhanced expressivity needed to parse
complex languages.

[§](https://docs.rs#getting-started)Getting started

The recommended way to start parsing with pest is to read the official [book](https://pest.rs/book).

Other helpful resources:

- API reference on [docs.rs](https://docs.rs/pest)
- play with grammars and share them on our [fiddle](https://pest.rs/#editor)
- find previous common questions answered or ask questions on [GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/pest-parser/pest/discussions)
- leave feedback, ask questions, or greet us on [Gitter](https://gitter.im/pest-parser/pest)or[Discord](https://discord.gg/XEGACtWpT2)

[§](https://docs.rs#pest-files)`.pest` files

Grammar definitions reside in custom `.pest` files located in the `src` directory. Their path is
relative to `src` and is specified between the `derive` attribute and empty `struct` that
`Parser` will be derived on.

[§](https://docs.rs#inline-grammars)Inline grammars

Grammars can also be inlined by using the `#[grammar_inline = "..."]` attribute.

[§](https://docs.rs#grammar)Grammar

A grammar is a series of rules separated by whitespace, possibly containing comments.

[§](https://docs.rs#comments)Comments

Comments start with `//` and end at the end of the line.

`// a comment`[§](https://docs.rs#rules)Rules

Rules have the following form:

The name of the rule is formed from alphanumeric characters or `_` with the condition that the
first character is not a digit and is used to create token pairs. When the rule starts being
parsed, the starting part of the token is being produced, with the ending part being produced
when the rule finishes parsing.

The following token pair notation `a(b(), c())` denotes the tokens: start `a`, start `b`, end
`b`, start `c`, end `c`, end `a`.

[§](https://docs.rs#modifiers)Modifiers

Modifiers are optional and can be one of `_`, `@`, `$`, or `!`. These modifiers change the
behavior of the rules.

-
Silent ( `_`)Silent rules do not create token pairs during parsing, nor are they error-reported. Parsing `"ab"`produces the token pair`b()`.
-
Atomic ( `@`)Atomic rules do not accept whitespace or comments within their expressions and have a cascading effect on any rule they call. I.e. rules that are not atomic but are called by atomic rules behave atomically. Any rules called by atomic rules do not generate token pairs. -

Expressions can be either terminals or non-terminals.

- Terminals

| Terminal | Usage |
|---|---|
| `"a"` | matches the exact string `"a"` |
| `^"a"` | matches the exact string `"a"`case insensitively (ASCII only) |
| `'a'..'z'` | matches one character between `'a'`and`'z'` |

| Non-terminal | Usage |
|---|---|

| `e*` | matches `e`zero or more times |
| `e+` | matches `e`one or more times |
| `e{n}` | matches `e`exactly`n`times |
| `e{, n}` | matches `e`at most`n`times |
| `e{n,}` | matches `e`at least`n`times |
| `e{m, n}` | matches `e`between`m`and`n`times inclusively |

| `&e` | matches `e`without making progress |

[§](https://docs.rs#special-rules)Special rules

- `WHITESPACE`- runs between rules and sub-rules
- `COMMENT`- runs between rules and sub-rules
- `ANY`- matches exactly one- `char`

# overseerd - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/overseerd/0.9.0/overseerd/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#overseerd)Overseerd

A component- and service-oriented framework. Depend on this single crate; it re-exports
the layered core — `overseerd-core` (vocabulary + resolver), `overseerd-di` (the DI
engine), `overseerd-hooks`, `overseerd-dirs`, `overseerd-config`, and `overseerd-app`
(the protocol-agnostic application core) — plus the procedural macros.

The native RPC daemon lives in its own `overseerd-rpc` crate and is re-exported here
behind the default-on ** daemon** feature (disable it with

`default-features = false`
for a core-framework-only build, or depend on `overseerd-rpc` directly).## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [builtins](https://docs.rs/builtins/index.html)
- Framework builtins: the seeded `ShutdownHandle``ServerConfig``LoggingConfig``init_tracing`subscriber helper.
- [client](https://docs.rs/client/index.html)
- The protocol-agnostic **client**core: the`ProtocolTransport``Client``app``daemon`, …) supplies a`ProtocolTransport`impl. Generated client code roots here, so it is identical across protocols.
- [config](https://docs.rs/config/index.html)
- Config source-format markers for `ConfigManager<F>`:`Toml``Dynamic``yaml`feature)`Yaml`.
- [daemon](https://docs.rs/daemon/index.html)
- The native RPC **daemon**plugin surface, namespaced so plugin items never collide with the facade root or with other plugins (`overseerd::axum::*`, …).
- [dirs](https://docs.rs/dirs/index.html)
- Application directory kinds (`Config`,`Data`,`Cache`,`State`,`Runtime`,`Tmp`), the typed`Dir``DirectoriesManager``Dir<dirs::Config>`.
- [prelude](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html)
- The common imports for the **core framework**:`use overseerd::prelude::*;`. Pair with`use overseerd::daemon::prelude::*;`(or another plugin’s prelude) for the protocol layer.
- [scope](https://docs.rs/scope/index.html)
- Component lifetime scopes: the `Scope``#[component(scope = Request)]`; a`#[component]`defaults to`Singleton`
- [transport](https://docs.rs/transport/index.html)
- The full transport substrate, including the framing codec and connection/responder types for building custom transports.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [app](https://docs.rs/macro.app.html)
- Assembles an app and validates it from one declaration.
- [daemon](https://docs.rs/macro.daemon.html)
- Deprecated alias for `app!`

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [App](https://docs.rs/struct.App.html)
- A fully assembled app, ready to serve its protocol.
- [AppBuilder](https://docs.rs/struct.AppBuilder.html)
- Assembles an `App`
- [AppRegistry](https://docs.rs/struct.AppRegistry.html)
- Holds the *agnostic*component, provider, and config-binding descriptors of an app — declarations only. Runtime instances live in the`ScopeContainer`
- [AppRuntime](https://docs.rs/struct.AppRuntime.html)
- Everything a protocol needs to drive requests through DI, cheaply cloneable.
- [Boxed](https://docs.rs/struct.BoxedComponent.html)- Component
- A type-erased instantiated component.
- [Cfg](https://docs.rs/struct.Cfg.html)
- An injected configuration value, bound from a property path.
- [CfgNext](https://docs.rs/struct.CfgNext.html)
- A **proposed**configuration value handed to a`#[hook(ConfigReload)]`method during a reload, before it is committed. Read-only; derefs to`T`. If every hook accepts the proposal the value is committed into its`Cfg<T>`
- [Changed](https://docs.rs/struct.ChangedBinding.html)- Binding
- One binding changed by a reload.
- [Component](https://docs.rs/struct.ComponentConstructionContext.html)- Construction - Context
- Context passed to a component factory during construction.
- [Component](https://docs.rs/struct.ComponentDescriptor.html)- Descriptor
- Static metadata describing a component and how to construct it.
- [Component](https://docs.rs/struct.ComponentFactoryDescriptor.html)- Factory - Descriptor
- One way to construct a component, carrying the dependencies *that constructor*needs (zero or many).
- [Component](https://docs.rs/struct.ComponentHookReport.html)- Hook - Report
- One component’s config-reload hook outcome.
- [Component](https://docs.rs/struct.ComponentRegistry.html)- Registry
- Holds the component and provider *descriptors*of an application — declarations only. Runtime instances live in the`ScopeContainer`
- [Component](https://docs.rs/struct.ComponentSource.html)- Source
- A `Resolver``ScopeContainer`
- [Config](https://docs.rs/struct.ConfigBinding.html)- Binding
- [Config](https://docs.rs/struct.ConfigBindingDescriptor.html)- Binding - Descriptor
- The link-time form of a `ConfigBinding``#[config(path = "..")]`so it is picked up by`ConfigManager::auto_discover``ConfigManager::with_config``Descriptor<ConfigBindingDescriptor>`.
- [Config](https://docs.rs/struct.ConfigManager.html)- Manager
- The merged configuration tree, owning the format it was read in.
- [Config](https://docs.rs/struct.ConfigReload.html)- Reload
- The config-reload hook kind: a `#[hook(ConfigReload)]`method runs when a config it targets is reloaded, receiving the proposed value(s) as`CfgNext<T>``HookOutcome`
- [Config](https://docs.rs/struct.ConfigReloadReport.html)- Reload - Report
- The outcome of a successful reload.
- [Config](https://docs.rs/struct.ConfigReloader.html)- Reloader
- A cheap, cloneable, injectable handle that re-reads configuration on demand.
- [Config](https://docs.rs/struct.ConfigStore.html)- Store
- A `Resolver``Cfg<T>`resolves through`ctx.get_resolver::<ConfigStore>()`rather than the component container. Bindings are deduped per`(type, path)`upstream, so the inner path map holds exactly one seed per path.
- [Dependency](https://docs.rs/struct.DependencyDescriptor.html)- Descriptor
- Declares that a component requires another component (or a config value).
- [Dir](https://docs.rs/struct.Dir.html)
- A resolved application directory of kind `K`, injectable by value.
- [Directories](https://docs.rs/struct.DirectoriesManager.html)- Manager
- Resolves and hands out the application’s `Dir<K>`
- [Directories](https://docs.rs/struct.DirectoriesResolver.html)- Resolver
- A `config::Resolver``@`directory namespace.
- [Dynamic](https://docs.rs/struct.Dynamic.html)
- Field wrapper marking a dependency as **runtime-provided**.
- [Flags](https://docs.rs/struct.Flags.html)
- Combinable control-flow flags carried in the flags section of a
`StatusCode`
- [Hook](https://docs.rs/struct.HookDescriptor.html)- Descriptor
- Static metadata for one hook, registered into its type’s `{Type}Hooks`slice.
- [Hook](https://docs.rs/struct.HookManager.html)- Manager
- Runs hooks of a kind against the live component instances.
- [Incoming](https://docs.rs/struct.IncomingCall.html)- Call
- An inbound RPC call received from the transport layer.
- [Live](https://docs.rs/struct.Live.html)
- A shared, swappable cell holding the current `Arc<T>`instance — the interior mutability primitive behind`Dep<T>``Cfg<T>`in the config layer).
- [LiveRef](https://docs.rs/struct.LiveRef.html)
- A guard pinning one generation of a `Live<T>``T`. Holding it keeps observing the generation current when`get``Live`, discouraging holding it across a long await (which would pin the old instance and delay a reload). Returned by both`Dep<T>``Cfg<T>`.
- [Logging](https://docs.rs/struct.LoggingConfig.html)- Config
- Tracing/logging settings consumed by the `init_tracing`helper, bound from a config subtree and injected as`Cfg<LoggingConfig>`
- [Memory](https://docs.rs/struct.MemoryCall.html)- Call
- A client-side handle to one in-flight call, covering all four kinds: send inbound items (client/bidi), receive server events, and cancel.
- [Memory](https://docs.rs/struct.MemoryClient.html)- Client
- The client side of an in-memory transport. Primarily used in tests.
- [Memory](https://docs.rs/struct.MemoryConnection.html)- Connection
- A logical in-memory connection. Yielded by `MemoryTransport::accept`.
- [Memory](https://docs.rs/struct.MemoryConnectionHandle.html)- Connection - Handle
- A handle representing one logical connection on the client side. Dropped when the client is done with the connection.
- [Memory](https://docs.rs/struct.MemoryResponder.html)- Responder
- Sends responses back through the call’s event channel (unary or streaming).
- [Memory](https://docs.rs/struct.MemoryTransport.html)- Transport
- The daemon side of an in-memory transport. Yields one `MemoryConnection`per`MemoryClient::connect`call.
- [Peer](https://docs.rs/struct.PeerInfo.html)- Info
- Transport-level information about the remote peer.
- [Provider](https://docs.rs/struct.ProviderDescriptor.html)- Descriptor
- Declares that a component **provides**a trait, so it can be injected as a single`Arc<dyn Trait>`(the primary or sole provider), or collected into a`Vec<Arc<dyn Trait>>`/`HashMap<String, Arc<dyn Trait>>`of all providers.
- [Reload](https://docs.rs/struct.ReloadProposal.html)- Proposal
- The proposed configuration handed to config-reload hooks: the staged value of every
binding (changed bindings hold their newly-deserialized value, unchanged bindings hold
their current value), so a hook’s `CfgNext<T>`
- [Reload](https://docs.rs/struct.ReloadTriggers.html)- Triggers
- Which automatic reload triggers a `ConfigManager``ConfigReloader::reload``serve`/`run`and spawns the matching background tasks.
- [Resolver](https://docs.rs/struct.ResolverSet.html)- Set
- A type-keyed bag of `Resolver``ResolverCtx`
- [Scope](https://docs.rs/struct.ScopeContainer.html)- Container
- One scope’s constructed instances, layered over an optional parent scope.
- [Server](https://docs.rs/struct.ServerConfig.html)- Config
- Network binding settings for a daemon’s transport, bound from a config subtree
and injected as `Cfg<ServerConfig>`
- [Shutdown](https://docs.rs/struct.Shutdown.html)
- Fired once when the daemon begins a graceful shutdown (the serve/run loop has stopped).
Errors from a `#[hook(Shutdown)]`are logged; shutdown proceeds regardless.
- [Shutdown](https://docs.rs/struct.ShutdownHandle.html)- Handle
- A cloneable handle for triggering graceful shutdown from any task.
- [Shutdown](https://docs.rs/struct.ShutdownSignal.html)- Signal
- Coordinates graceful daemon shutdown across all tasks in the process.
- [Startup](https://docs.rs/struct.Startup.html)
- Fired once after the daemon is built and before it begins serving. An `Err`from any`#[hook(Startup)]`aborts startup — the daemon does not begin accepting work.
- [Status](https://docs.rs/struct.StatusCode.html)- Code
- A structured status code carried on every error response.
- [Stream](https://docs.rs/struct.StreamDecodeError.html)- Decode - Error
- A failure decoding a wire frame back into a stream item.
- [Stream](https://docs.rs/struct.StreamEncodeError.html)- Encode - Error
- A failure encoding a stream item into a wire frame. Carries the `StatusCode`and body the terminating`StreamError`frame will report, mirroring the handler-side error currency so a custom codec can classify its own failures.
- [TcpTransport](https://docs.rs/struct.TcpTransport.html)
- TCP transport. Each accepted connection handles calls sequentially.
- [Type](https://docs.rs/struct.TypeDescriptor.html)- Descriptor
- Static metadata describing a Rust type, safe to embed in `'static`descriptors.
- [Unix](https://docs.rs/struct.UnixTransport.html)- Transport
- Unix socket transport. Removes the socket file on drop.
- [Wire](https://docs.rs/struct.WireRequest.html)- Request
- The request half of the wire protocol, also the opening frame of a stream.
- [Wire](https://docs.rs/struct.WireResponse.html)- Response
- The response half of the wire protocol.
- [Wiring](https://docs.rs/struct.Wiring.html)
- The crate-wide anchor that each component’s `Provide`impl attaches to. A dependency assertion is the bound`Wiring: Provide<Dep>`.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Call](https://docs.rs/enum.CallResult.html)- Result
- Success or failure of an RPC call at the transport layer.
- [Cardinality](https://docs.rs/enum.Cardinality.html)
- Cardinality of a dependency edge: how many values satisfy it.
- [Config](https://docs.rs/enum.ConfigError.html)- Error
- Errors from loading, merging, and binding configuration.
- [Config](https://docs.rs/enum.ConfigReloadError.html)- Reload - Error
- Errors from a configuration reload. On any error the live values are left untouched — a reload commits only when every changed binding re-binds and every affected hook accepts.
- [Default](https://docs.rs/enum.DefaultSpec.html)- Spec
- The shape of a config type’s field defaults, emitted by the `#[config]`macro and consumed by the merge step.
- [DiError](https://docs.rs/enum.DiError.html)
- The DI layer’s own error/result, exposed under distinct names so macro-generated
**factory**code can name them without colliding with the root [`Error`]/`Result`
- [EnumTag](https://docs.rs/enum.EnumTag.html)
- How an enum is tagged, so the merge can synthesize the same shape serde deserializes.
- [Hook](https://docs.rs/enum.HookError.html)- Error
- The hook layer’s own error/result, exposed under distinct names so macro-generated hook
code can name them without colliding with the root [`Error`]/`Result`*domain*outcome (e.g. whether a config reload is accepted) is its`HookKind::Output`
- [Hook](https://docs.rs/enum.HookOutcome.html)- Outcome
- What a `#[hook(ConfigReload)]`hook reports back.`Err`from the hook aborts the reload; these variants all mean the proposal was accepted.
- [Predefined](https://docs.rs/enum.PredefinedCode.html)- Code
- The framework-owned category occupying the predefined section of a
`StatusCode`
- [Server](https://docs.rs/enum.ServerEvent.html)- Event
- A server→client event for one call. Unary calls produce a single
`Response`; streaming calls produce`Item`s terminated by`End`or`Error`.
- [Wire](https://docs.rs/enum.WireMessage.html)- Message
- Top-level wire message. Every frame on the wire is one of these.
- [Wire](https://docs.rs/enum.WireOutcome.html)- Outcome
- Success or failure at the wire level.

## Statics[§](https://docs.rs#statics)

- [COMPONENTS](https://docs.rs/static.COMPONENTS.html)
- Link-time registry of every discovered `ComponentDescriptor`
- [CONFIG_](https://docs.rs/static.CONFIG_BINDINGS.html)- BINDINGS
- Link-time registry of every auto-registered config binding (a `#[config(path = "..")]`type), collected by`ConfigManager::auto_discover`
- [PROVIDERS](https://docs.rs/static.PROVIDERS.html)

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Component](https://docs.rs/trait.Component.html)
- Metadata trait for types registerable as components.
- [Component](https://docs.rs/trait.ComponentFactories.html)- Factories
- A component type’s own construction factories.
- [Component](https://docs.rs/trait.ComponentHooks.html)- Hooks
- A component type’s own hooks.
- [Config](https://docs.rs/trait.ConfigDefaults.html)- Defaults
- Runtime, object-safe access to a config type’s `DefaultSpec`
- [Config](https://docs.rs/trait.ConfigProperties.html)- Properties
- A struct bindable from a configuration subtree, injectable as `Cfg<Self>`
- [Connection](https://docs.rs/trait.Connection.html)
- A live session between the daemon and one remote peer.
- [Container](https://docs.rs/trait.ContainerConfigExt.html)- Config - Ext
- Ad-hoc config access from a built container: the relocated `.config()`accessor.
- [Descriptor](https://docs.rs/trait.Descriptor.html)
- Connects a type to a static descriptor of kind `D`, enabling type-to-descriptor lookups where the type is known but its link-time descriptor would otherwise only be reachable through a slice.
- [DirKind](https://docs.rs/trait.DirKind.html)
- A kind of application directory. Implemented by the marker types and used by
`DirectoriesManager``Dir<Self>`
- [Factory](https://docs.rs/trait.Factory.html)
- An async factory function whose parameters are all `FromContainer``FactoryOutput``Args`is the parameter-tuple marker that selects the arity impl.
- [Factory](https://docs.rs/trait.FactoryOutput.html)- Output
- What a factory function may return: the component itself, or a `Result`of it.
- [From](https://docs.rs/trait.FromContainer.html)- Container
- A single factory parameter, resolvable from the construction context, that reports the dependency edge it represents.
- [Hook](https://docs.rs/trait.HookKind.html)- Kind
- A kind of hook: the event a `#[hook(Kind)]`method reacts to.
- [Hook](https://docs.rs/trait.HookParam.html)- Param
- A parameter a `#[hook(K)]`method may take: an input of kind`K`, extracted from the kind’s context — never a component dependency (those come through`&self`).
- [Injectable](https://docs.rs/trait.Injectable.html)
- How a resolved dependency is stored in, and handed out of, the container.
- [Plugin](https://docs.rs/trait.Plugin.html)
- A general extension unit applied to an app while it is built.
- [Protocol](https://docs.rs/trait.Protocol.html)
- A pluggable serve/dispatch layer over the app’s DI runtime. There is exactly one
active protocol per `App`.
- [Protocol](https://docs.rs/trait.ProtocolPlugin.html)- Plugin
- A `Plugin``Protocol``App`is built around exactly one of these.
- [Provide](https://docs.rs/trait.Provide.html)
- Compile-time dependency marker: `Wiring: Provide<T>`holds when some component in scope provides`T`. Under the`di-check`feature, the macros emit`impl Provide<Self> for Wiring`for every component and a bound per concrete dependency, so a missing provider is a`cargo check`error.
- [Reloadable](https://docs.rs/trait.ReloadableConfig.html)- Config
- A config binding the reloader can re-bind: it knows its path, how to re-deserialize its
type from a re-read tree, and how to stage its current value. Object-safe so the
reloader holds a `Vec<Box<dyn ReloadableConfig>>`across all bound types.
- [Resolver](https://docs.rs/trait.Resolver.html)
- A source of resolved values of one kind (components, config, …).
- [Resolver](https://docs.rs/trait.ResolverCtx.html)- Ctx
- A type-keyed set of `Resolver`
- [Resolver](https://docs.rs/trait.ResolverCtxExt.html)- CtxExt
- Ergonomic, generic accessor over a `ResolverCtx``&dyn ResolverCtx`) gets`ctx.get_resolver::<R>()`for free.
- [Respond](https://docs.rs/trait.Respond.html)
- Sends the single response back to the caller of a unary inbound RPC.
- [Respond](https://docs.rs/trait.RespondStream.html)- Stream
- Converts a responder into a multi-item sink for server- and bidirectional-
streaming calls. Consuming the responder this way replaces the single
`respond`with a stream of items terminated by`finish`or`error`.
- [Response](https://docs.rs/trait.ResponseSink.html)- Sink
- The outbound half of a streaming call: many items followed by exactly one
terminator. `send`awaits when the peer is slow, providing backpressure.
- [Scope](https://docs.rs/trait.Scope.html)
- A lifetime scope label: where a component instance is stored and how long it lives.
- [Serve](https://docs.rs/trait.Serve.html)
- Serves a built protocol over a concrete endpoint type `E`. Kept separate from`Protocol``SocketAddr`. The serve loop only needs to watch`endpoint`and`shutdown`; lifecycle and reload are handled by the caller (`App::serve`).
- [Service](https://docs.rs/trait.ServiceComponent.html)- Component
- A `Component`
- [Static](https://docs.rs/trait.StaticScope.html)- Scope
- Ergonomic authoring sugar for a zero-sized scope: provide the three associated
constants and a `Scope``Connection`,`Request`, a custom`#[scope]`) declare themselves this way.
- [Stream](https://docs.rs/trait.StreamDecode.html)- Decode
- The receive half of a stream item’s wire format: how frame bytes become an item.
- [Stream](https://docs.rs/trait.StreamEncode.html)- Encode
- The send half of a stream item’s wire format: how an item becomes frame bytes.
- [Transport](https://docs.rs/trait.Transport.html)
- An abstract source of inbound connections.
- [Wired](https://docs.rs/trait.Wired.html)
- Marker that all of a component’s dependencies are provided. Under `di-check`the macros emit`impl Wired for T where Wiring: Provide<Dep>, ..`carrying*every*single dependency (concrete and trait-object) as a lazy bound.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [dispatch_](https://docs.rs/fn.dispatch_factory.html)- factory
- Drives `factory`to a boxed component, erased to the`ComponentFactory`
- [factory_](https://docs.rs/fn.factory_dependencies.html)- dependencies
- The dependency edges of `factory`, recovered from its`Factory``Args`; the macro wraps a non-capturing call to this in the`fn() -> Vec<..>`the descriptor stores.
- [from_](https://docs.rs/fn.from_boxed.html)- boxed
- Recovers handle `H`from a boxed slot: downcasts to its stored representation (`H::Stored`) and derives the handle. This is the single seam through which every resolution converts storage back into a handle — a snapshot for`Arc<T>`, a shared clone for`Dep<T>`, a plain clone for a by-value handle.`None`if the box holds a different stored type.
- [no_](https://docs.rs/fn.no_hooks.html)- hooks
- The empty hooks slice for a type that declares none — the default carried by a
`ComponentDescriptor`.
- [spawn_](https://docs.rs/fn.spawn_reload_triggers.html)- reload_ - triggers
- Spawns the background tasks for the requested triggers, returning their handles so the
caller can abort them on shutdown. Unsupported requests (SIGHUP off-Unix, watching
without the `watch`feature) are logged and skipped.
- [type_](https://docs.rs/fn.type_id_of.html)- id_ - of
- Returns the TypeId of T. Used as a function pointer in TypeDescriptor.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [CallId](https://docs.rs/type.CallId.html)
- Opaque identifier correlating a request to its response within a connection.
- [Component](https://docs.rs/type.ComponentContainer.html)- Container
- Backwards-compatible alias: the root singleton store is a `ScopeContainer`
- [Component](https://docs.rs/type.ComponentFactory.html)- Factory
- Async factory function pointer for constructing a component.
- [Dep](https://docs.rs/type.Dep.html)
- A reloadable dependency handle: a stable handle to a component slot whose instance may be swapped at runtime (e.g. by a config reload).
- [DiResult](https://docs.rs/type.DiResult.html)
- The DI layer’s own error/result, exposed under distinct names so macro-generated
**factory**code can name them without colliding with the root [`Error`]/`Result`
- [Hook](https://docs.rs/type.HookCall.html)- Call
- The erased call shape every hook is compiled to: resolve the receiver (if the method
takes `&self`) from the resolver context, extract the kind’s params from the erased context, run the method, and box its output. The boxed value is always the kind’s`Output`.
- [Hook](https://docs.rs/type.HookResult.html)- Result
- The hook layer’s own error/result, exposed under distinct names so macro-generated hook
code can name them without colliding with the root [`Error`]/`Result`

## Attribute Macros[§](https://docs.rs#attributes)

- [component](https://docs.rs/attr.component.html)
- Declares a **system-constructed singleton component**on a struct.
- [config](https://docs.rs/attr.config.html)
- Implements the `ConfigProperties`trait for a config`struct`or`enum`, making it injectable as`Cfg<T>`from a property path.
- [injectable](https://docs.rs/attr.injectable.html)
- Marks a trait as injectable as `Arc<dyn Trait>`(providers register with`#[component(provide = dyn Trait)]`).
- [methods](https://docs.rs/attr.methods.html)
- Registers a component’s lifecycle methods from an inherent `impl`block.

# tatara_build_remote - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/tatara-build-remote/0.2.120/tatara_build_remote/

## Expand description

`tatara-build-remote` — layered Nix build transport for tatara guests.

Takes a `BuildRef` (flake + attr, raw Nix expression, store path, or
OCI image) and resolves it to a concrete `StorePath` using a
priority-ordered chain of transports. **First match wins.** Default
chain:

- **Attic cache**— pulls from a shared Attic instance (e.g.- `quero.lol`). Fastest path when the artifact is already cached.
- **ssh-ng remote builder**— submits to a remote Nix builder over- `ssh-ng://`. Used when Attic misses and the local machine can’t or shouldn’t build (cross-arch, resource constrained, etc.).
- **Local**—- `nix build`on the host. Last resort.

Any transport declared absent in the spec is skipped. If all declared
transports fail, `BuildError::AllTransportsFailed` bubbles up and
hospedeiro refuses to boot the guest — we fail closed.

[§](https://docs.rs#status)Status

**Phase H.5 landed.** `AtticTransport`, `SshRemoteTransport`, and
`LocalTransport` all ship in `transports.rs`.
`BuildTransportChain::to_layered()` composes them into a priority-
ordered `LayeredTransport` driven by `(defguest …)`’s `:build-on`
keyword.

[§](https://docs.rs#why-layered-not-single-target)Why layered, not single-target

The fleet at `quero.lol` has a shared Attic cache *and* an ssh-ng
builder pool. Cache hits are free; builds are expensive. Layering
lets the common case (pleme-io team members pulling pre-built
artifacts) skip the slow path entirely. Keys + SSH config come from
the cid node’s `pangea-builder.nix` — no new auth plumbing.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use transports::`- [AtticTransport](https://docs.rs/transports/struct.AtticTransport.html);
- `pub use transports::`- [LocalTransport](https://docs.rs/transports/struct.LocalTransport.html);
- `pub use transports::`- [SshRemoteTransport](https://docs.rs/transports/struct.SshRemoteTransport.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [transports](https://docs.rs/transports/index.html)
- Concrete `BuildTransport`implementations.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Build](https://docs.rs/struct.BuildTransportChain.html)- Transport - Chain
- Declarative transport chain. A `None`field means “don’t try this transport”.
- [Layered](https://docs.rs/struct.LayeredTransport.html)- Transport
- Layered transport — tries each child in order, returns the first success.
- [Store](https://docs.rs/struct.StorePath.html)- Path
- A Nix store path — content-addressed handle.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Build](https://docs.rs/enum.BuildError.html)- Error
- [Build](https://docs.rs/enum.BuildRef.html)- Ref
- A reference to something that becomes a Nix store path.

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [CRATE_](https://docs.rs/constant.CRATE_STATUS.html)- STATUS
- Phase marker. Bumped by each phase that lands a change.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Build](https://docs.rs/trait.BuildTransport.html)- Transport
- The operation-level transport trait. Phase H.5 implements
`AtticTransport`,`SshRemoteTransport`, and`LocalTransport`.

# tatara_lisp_derive - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/tatara-lisp-derive/0.2.120/tatara_lisp_derive/

## Expand description

`#[derive(TataraDomain)]` — generate a `TataraDomain` impl from a Rust struct.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use tatara_lisp_derive::TataraDomain;
#[derive(TataraDomain)]
#[tatara(keyword = "defmonitor")]
pub struct MonitorSpec {
    pub name: String,
    pub query: String,
    pub threshold: f64,
    pub window_seconds: Option<i64>,
}
```
Generates:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
impl TataraDomain for MonitorSpec {
    const KEYWORD: &'static str = "defmonitor";
    fn compile_from_args(args: &[Sexp]) -> Result<Self> {
        let kw = parse_kwargs_strict(args, __TATARA_ALLOWED_KEYWORDS)?;
        Ok(Self {
            name: extract_string(&kw, "name")?.to_string(),
            query: extract_string(&kw, "query")?.to_string(),
            threshold: extract_float(&kw, "threshold")?,
            window_seconds: extract_optional_int(&kw, "window-seconds")?,
        })
    }
}
```
Invoked from Lisp:

`(defmonitor :name "prom-up" :query "up{…}" :threshold 0.99 :window-seconds 300)`Supported field types (v0):

- `String`,- `Option<String>`,- `Vec<String>`
- `i64`,- `i32`,- `u32`,- `usize`,- `u64`,- `Option<i64>`
- `f64`,- `f32`,- `Option<f64>`
- `bool`,- `Option<bool>`

## Derive Macros[§](https://docs.rs#derives)
