# awsm_renderer_glb_export - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/awsm-renderer-glb-export/0.13.0/awsm_renderer_glb_export/

## Expand description

Scene-complete glTF/GLB **export** IR + writer.

This crate is the one-way bake target: an editor project (any mix of
procedural recipes, raw-edited meshes, and imported models) is flattened to
triangles + materials and handed here as a [ GlbScene](https://docs.rs/struct.GlbScene.html), which

[serializes to a self-contained](https://docs.rs/fn.write_glb.html)

`write_glb``.glb` byte vector.It has **no GPU / editor / wasm dependencies** — only `awsm-renderer-meshgen` (for the
plain-data [ MeshData](https://docs.rs/struct.MeshData.html)) and

`gltf-json` (the JSON model used to *build*a glTF). That keeps the whole writer natively unit-testable (

`cargo test -p awsm-renderer-glb-export`).[§](https://docs.rs#scene-complete-by-design)Scene-complete by design

The IR carries node hierarchy + transforms, meshes, materials, **lights**,
**cameras**, **animations**, and an **environment** slot up front — even
though the standalone Phase-1 export path only populates mesh + material. The
player-bundle publish path (Phase 6) reuses the exact same IR + writer for the
whole-runtime bake, so the shape must not be mesh-only.

[§](https://docs.rs#material-policy-lossless-portable)Material policy (lossless, portable)

- Built-in **PBR**→ real glTF PBR (`ExportMaterial::Pbr`
- **Unlit**→- `KHR_materials_unlit`(- `ExportMaterial::Unlit`
- **Non-PBR**(custom WGSL / Toon / anything not glTF-representable) →- `ExportMaterial::None`- `AWSM_MATERIALS_NONE`- **no embedded material**, so a re-import leaves the material slot empty for scene-level resolution.
- **Textures are referenced-only**: the writer embeds exactly the images present in- `GlbScene::images`- *assigned*materials use, so reassigning a lighter material drops the heavy textures with no special “slim” flag.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [EnvRef](https://docs.rs/struct.EnvRef.html)
- Environment references (skybox / IBL). Written to a sidecar by the player bundle (Phase 6); glTF itself carries no IBL.
- [Export](https://docs.rs/struct.ExportAnimChannel.html)- Anim - Channel
- One animation channel: a sampler (times → values) bound to a node TRS / morph target.
- [Export](https://docs.rs/struct.ExportAnimation.html)- Animation
- A keyframe animation. Lowered to glTF animations on write.
- [Export](https://docs.rs/struct.ExportImage.html)- Image
- An embedded image (referenced-only). Stored in the GLB `BIN`chunk via a buffer view +`image.mimeType`.
- [Export](https://docs.rs/struct.ExportNode.html)- Node
- One node in the export forest.
- [Export](https://docs.rs/struct.ExportSkin.html)- Skin
- A skin (skeleton) — a set of joint nodes + their inverse-bind matrices. The
player rebuilds the skinned deformation from this + the mesh’s per-vertex
`JOINTS_0`/`WEIGHTS_0`; our clips animate the joint nodes’ TRS.
- [Extra](https://docs.rs/struct.ExtraPrimitive.html)- Primitive
- An additional primitive on an `ExportNode``ExportNode::extra_primitives``weights`array shared by all primitives); a valid source glTF guarantees this.
- [Extracted](https://docs.rs/struct.ExtractedMorph.html)- Morph
- One node’s morph-target set, extracted alongside its geometry. Carries raw per-target position/normal deltas (tangent deltas are dropped — the renderer zero-fills that slot) + the default per-target weights; the packing method produces the exact byte layout the renderer’s geometry-morph store consumes.
- [Extracted](https://docs.rs/struct.ExtractedNodeMesh.html)- Node - Mesh
- Read the geometry of a single glTF node out of an already-loaded
`gltf::Document``MeshData`
- [Extracted](https://docs.rs/struct.ExtractedSkin.html)- Skin
- One node’s skin (rig) binding, extracted alongside its geometry. Mirrors the
shapes the renderer’s `RawSkin`+`Skins::insert`consume;`joint_node_indices`are glTF node indices (mapped to editor`TransformKey`s by the caller).
- [GlbScene](https://docs.rs/struct.GlbScene.html)
- The root of an export: a node forest plus scene-wide animation, environment, and the referenced-only image pool.
- [Mesh](https://docs.rs/struct.MeshData.html)- Data
- Plain-data mesh representation. The renderer’s raw-mesh API consumes this directly.
- [Morph](https://docs.rs/struct.MorphTarget.html)- Target
- One morph target: per-vertex position (and optional normal) **deltas**added to the base mesh, scaled by the target’s weight. Parallel to the mesh’s vertices.
- [PbrMaterial](https://docs.rs/struct.PbrMaterial.html)
- glTF metallic-roughness PBR parameters. All textures are optional refs into
`GlbScene::images`
- [TexRef](https://docs.rs/struct.TexRef.html)
- A reference from a material slot to an image in `GlbScene::images`
- [TexTransform](https://docs.rs/struct.TexTransform.html)
- `KHR_texture_transform`— a UV offset/rotation/scale (+ optional texcoord override) on a single textureInfo. Carried on- `TexRef`
- [Trs](https://docs.rs/struct.Trs.html)
- A translate / rotate (xyzw quaternion) / scale local transform. Mirrors
`awsm_renderer_scene::Trs`but kept local so this crate stays decoupled from the project schema.
- [Unlit](https://docs.rs/struct.UnlitMaterial.html)- Material
- `KHR_materials_unlit`material — only the base color (factor + optional texture) is meaningful.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Alpha](https://docs.rs/enum.AlphaMode.html)- Mode
- glTF alpha rendering mode.
- [Anim](https://docs.rs/enum.AnimInterp.html)- Interp
- [Anim](https://docs.rs/enum.AnimPath.html)- Path
- [Export](https://docs.rs/enum.ExportCamera.html)- Camera
- glTF camera projection.
- [Export](https://docs.rs/enum.ExportLight.html)- Light
- Punctual light (`KHR_lights_punctual`). glTF directional/point/spot.
- [Export](https://docs.rs/enum.ExportMaterial.html)- Material
- How a material is emitted into the glTF. See the crate-level material policy.
- [Image](https://docs.rs/enum.ImageMime.html)- Mime

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [AWSM_](https://docs.rs/constant.AWSM_MATERIALS_NONE.html)- MATERIALS_ - NONE
- The primitive-level glTF extension marking a primitive whose real material is
**not**glTF-representable and must be resolved by the scene/player on import (rather than defaulting to a glTF material). Defined here once; the importer (`renderer-gltf`) recognizes the same token to leave the material slot empty.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [extract_](https://docs.rs/fn.extract_node_mesh.html)- node_ - mesh
- [extract_](https://docs.rs/fn.extract_node_mesh_from_bytes.html)- node_ - mesh_ - from_ - bytes
- Parse glTF/GLB bytes and extract one node’s geometry in a single call — the editor’s export path uses this on the cached source bytes of an imported model.
- [extract_](https://docs.rs/fn.extract_node_mesh_with_skin_from_bytes.html)- node_ - mesh_ - with_ - skin_ - from_ - bytes
- Like `extract_node_mesh_from_bytes``ExtractedNodeMesh``ExtractedSkin``assets/<source>.glb`) at a node to rebuild its skinned drawable (geometry + skin) from our-format. Self-contained sources only (embedded / data-URI buffers — the rig glb is single-BIN).
- [extract_](https://docs.rs/fn.extract_texture_images.html)- texture_ - images
- Extract the ENCODED image bytes (the original PNG/JPEG) of every glTF
TEXTURE, keyed by glTF texture index. Reuses the clean-export [`ImagePool`] resolution: GLB buffer-view or`data:`URI sources only (external-file URIs can’t be resolved from bytes, and non-PNG/JPEG mimes are skipped — those texture indices are simply absent from the map).
- [extract_](https://docs.rs/fn.extract_texture_images_from_bytes.html)- texture_ - images_ - from_ - bytes
- Bytes wrapper for `extract_texture_images`
- [extract_](https://docs.rs/fn.extract_texture_images_with_external.html)- texture_ - images_ - with_ - external
- `extract_texture_images`- `encoded_images`(indexed by glTF image index). The plain- `(doc, buffers)`form can only recover embedded buffer-view /- `data:`URI images; an external-URI texture’s bytes live ONLY in- `encoded_images`, so without this the editor never captures them → empty- `content_hash`→ the texture silently drops on save→reload. Pass the import’s- `data.encoded_images`.
- [reexport_](https://docs.rs/fn.reexport_clean.html)- clean
- Re-export a source glTF/GLB into a **clean**`GlbScene`**materials and their textures**(core PBR / unlit factors + the referenced images, copied as their original encoded PNG/JPEG bytes — no re-encode), with animations, cameras, and lights dropped. Materials stay PER PRIMITIVE: a multi-material source mesh becomes one primitive per material on the SAME node (see`ExportNode::extra_primitives``write_glb``assets/<id>.glb`(the “re-export everything through our writer” path: uniform encoding, no orphaned accessors).
- [reexport_](https://docs.rs/fn.reexport_clean_scene.html)- clean_ - scene
- Like `reexport_clean``gltf::Document`
- [reexport_](https://docs.rs/fn.reexport_clean_scene_with_images.html)- clean_ - scene_ - with_ - images
- Like `reexport_clean_scene``GltfData.encoded_images`, by glTF image index) so EXTERNAL-file images — which can’t be resolved from`(doc, buffers)`alone — still round-trip into the clean glb. Pass`&[]`for the embedded-only behaviour. This is how model-tests (and any importer of external-image glTF) makes textures survive the our-format conversion.
- [scene_](https://docs.rs/fn.scene_node_flat_indices.html)- node_ - flat_ - indices
- Map each source glTF node index → its index in the **clean re-export**: the depth-first (root-first, children in order) flatten over the default scene, exactly the order`reexport_clean_scene``GlbScene::nodes``write_glb`
- [write_](https://docs.rs/fn.write_glb.html)- glb

# overseerd_rpc_macros - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/overseerd-rpc-macros/0.9.0/overseerd_rpc_macros/

## Expand description

The Overseerd **RPC daemon** macros: `#[service]`, `#[handlers]`, `#[rpc]`, and
`app!`/`daemon!`. They are RPC-protocol-specific (they emit `::overseerd::daemon::*` types),
so they live in their own crate rather than the core `overseerd-macros`, built on the shared
[ overseerd_macros_core](https://docs.rs/overseerd-macros-core/0.9.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/overseerd_macros_core/index.html) codegen.

Re-exported through the `overseerd` facade’s `daemon` module; depend on the facade, not this
crate directly.

- `#[service]`is a- **router component**: a- `#[component]`(field-injected singleton) plus a service header, its- `{Service}Rpcs`slice, and the generated client struct.
- `#[handlers]`is- `MethodArgs<Rpcs>`— the base impl macro (- `#[methods]`:- `#[init]`+- `#[hook]`) plus the RPC extension, which registers each- `#[rpc]`method and contributes the client methods.
- `#[rpc]`marks a method inside a- `#[handlers]`impl (a marker stripped by- `#[handlers]`).

`app!`/`daemon!` are **not** here — they are protocol-agnostic core macros (in
`overseerd-macros`), selecting a protocol via a required `protocol:` field.

## Attribute Macros[§](https://docs.rs#attributes)

- [handlers](https://docs.rs/attr.handlers.html)
- Contributes the `#[rpc]`methods (and an optional`#[init]`/`#[hook]`s) of an inherent`impl`block to the service of`Self`.
- [rpc](https://docs.rs/attr.rpc.html)
- Marks a method inside a `#[handlers]`impl as an RPC. A**marker**consumed and stripped by`#[handlers]`; used on its own it emits a`compile_error!`.
- [service](https://docs.rs/attr.service.html)
- Declares a **service**— a router component exposing RPC methods.

---

# overseerd_axum - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/overseerd-axum/0.9.0/overseerd_axum/

## Expand description

The Overseerd axum/HTTP protocol, built on the protocol-agnostic `overseerd-app` core.

This crate is a [ ProtocolPlugin](https://docs.rs/trait.ProtocolPlugin.html): it builds a real

[from](https://docs.rs/axum/0.8.9/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/axum/routing/struct.Router.html)

`axum::Router``#[controller]`
components, bridges the framework’s dependency injection into axum via the [extractor (so route handlers mix native axum extractors with DI), and serves over HTTP. Depend on it directly, or reach it through the](https://docs.rs/extract/struct.Inject.html)

`Inject``overseerd` facade’s `axum` feature.The DI bridge is deliberately thin and one-directional: nothing in `overseerd-di` or
`overseerd-core` knows axum exists. A per-request scope layer threads an
[ Arc<ScopeContainer>](https://docs.rs/overseerd-di/0.9.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/overseerd_di/container/struct.ScopeContainer.html) through the request extensions, and

[resolves components from it.](https://docs.rs/extract/struct.Inject.html)

`Inject`## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

# overseerd_client - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/overseerd-client/0.9.0/overseerd_client/

## Expand description

The Overseerd protocol-agnostic client *contract*.

The framework implements no client calls. It defines **capabilities** a protocol may
support — one trait each — and a protocol (`overseerd-rpc`, a future HTTP binding, …)
implements the subset it can. A protocol *declares* support by implementing a capability
and *refuses* by simply not: a client-streaming call over HTTP/1.1 is then a compile
error — a protocol limitation expressed in the type system, never a framework limit.

| Capability | trait | HTTP/1.1 | HTTP/2 | gRPC | custom RPC |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| one req → one resp | `Unary` | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| one req → many resp | `ServerStreaming` | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| many req → one resp | `ClientStreaming` | — | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| many req ↔ many resp | `BidiStreaming` | — | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |

The protocol owns **everything** behind each method: body encoding and parsing, framing,
routing, and streaming. A streaming capability returns the protocol’s own response
[ Stream](https://docs.rs/futures-core/0.3.32/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/futures_core/stream/trait.Stream.html) as an associated type — a real contract that the result

*is*a stream of decoded items, not an opaque box that would pretend any stream fits.

A generated client (`FooClient<C>`) bounds `C` on exactly the capabilities its RPCs need
and delegates to them, so the same generated code runs over any protocol providing those
capabilities.

The framework assumes **no serialization**: it never bounds a message on `serde` (a
protocol might use rkyv, protobuf, …). Instead a protocol declares what it can carry by
implementing [ Encodes<T>](https://docs.rs/trait.Encodes.html) /

[for those message types (typically a blanket](https://docs.rs/trait.Decodes.html)

`Decodes<T>``impl<T: Serialize> Encodes<T>`, or `impl<T: Archive> Encodes<T>`, …). A capability method
is bound `where Self: Encodes<Req> + Decodes<Resp>`, so a message the protocol cannot
serialize is a compile error — protocol-defined, never framework-assumed.## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Codec](https://docs.rs/struct.CodecError.html)- Error
- A body encode/decode failure. Carries a `StatusCode``BadInput`) and a human-readable message.
- [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.ErrorBody.html)- Body
- The client mirror of the server’s error response: a protocol-defined status `S`plus the raw error body bytes. The status is opaque to the framework (the protocol picks`S`; RPC uses its packed`transport::StatusCode`, HTTP uses`http::StatusCode`) — only the caller interprets it. The body is deserialized into`T`lazily and best-effort, so a body the handler serialized as a different type (or as raw, non-postcard bytes) degrades to a failed`deserialize`while`code`/`raw`stay usable.
- [Raw](https://docs.rs/struct.Raw.html)
- Marker for an error body whose payload type is not known statically (the generic call path). Typed clients substitute the method’s declared error type.
- [Stream](https://docs.rs/struct.StreamArg.html)- Arg
- A boxed input stream a streaming-request capability accepts. Build one from any `Stream`with`.into()`(or`new`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Client](https://docs.rs/enum.ClientError.html)- Error
- Everything that can go wrong on a client call. Generic over the error body type `E`so typed clients surface an`ErrorBody<E>``deserialize``Raw`

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Bidi](https://docs.rs/trait.BidiStreaming.html)- Streaming
- A bidirectional stream of requests and responses (HTTP/2, gRPC, custom RPC — *not*HTTP/1.1). The request stream is pumped concurrently with reading the response stream.
- [Client](https://docs.rs/trait.ClientStreaming.html)- Streaming
- A stream of requests, one response (HTTP/2, gRPC, custom RPC — *not*HTTP/1.1, which has no streamed request body, so it does not implement this trait).
- [Decodes](https://docs.rs/trait.Decodes.html)
- A protocol can decode a `T`(a request, response, or stream item) from a wire body.
- [Encodes](https://docs.rs/trait.Encodes.html)
- A protocol can encode a `T`(a request, response, or stream item) into a wire body. Implemented by a protocol for the message types it supports.
- [Server](https://docs.rs/trait.ServerStreaming.html)- Streaming
- One request, a stream of responses (HTTP/1.1 chunked/SSE, HTTP/2, gRPC, custom RPC). The
response stream is the protocol’s own type — a contract that the result *is*a`Stream`
- [Transport](https://docs.rs/trait.Transport.html)
- The base every capability shares: a transport carries a protocol-defined `Status``transport::StatusCode`; HTTP sets it to`http::StatusCode`. Every capability requires this, so a transport declares its status once and it threads through every call shape’s errors.
- [Unary](https://docs.rs/trait.Unary.html)
- One request, one response. Every protocol supports this. The implementation owns body
encoding (via `Encodes``Decodes`

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [retype](https://docs.rs/fn.retype.html)
- Re-labels an untyped error onto a typed error of the same shape, preserving its status `S`. The only arm carrying`E`is`Remote`, whose body bytes are re-marked, not re-decoded. Used by protocol impls and generated clients.

# rpic_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rpic-core/0.4.0/rpic_core/

## Expand description

rpic-core — engine for the `pic` picture-drawing language.

Pipeline: source → [ lexer](https://docs.rs/lexer/index.html) →

[→](https://docs.rs/parser/index.html)

`parser`[→ [](https://docs.rs/ast/index.html)

`ast``eval`] → placed
primitives ([) → render backends (](https://docs.rs/ir/index.html)

`ir`[, later PNG/PDF). This crate is pure (no file I/O); the CLI and WASM wrappers drive it.](https://docs.rs/svg/index.html)

`svg`Note: [`eval`] is the pic-language *interpreter* — a safe walker over a typed
expression/geometry tree. It executes no arbitrary code.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [ast](https://docs.rs/ast/index.html)
- Abstract syntax tree for the pic language.
- [eval](https://docs.rs/eval/index.html)
- Evaluator: walks the `crate::ast``Drawing`
- [geom](https://docs.rs/geom/index.html)
- Geometry primitives. pic works in a Cartesian plane with y pointing up; internal units are pic “inches” (scaled to device units by each backend).
- [ir](https://docs.rs/ir/index.html)
- Intermediate representation: the placed-primitive tree produced by the evaluator and consumed by the render backends. All coordinates are absolute, in pic units (inches), y pointing up.
- [lexer](https://docs.rs/lexer/index.html)
- Hand-written lexer for the pic language.
- [parser](https://docs.rs/parser/index.html)
- Recursive-descent parser for the pic drawing core.
- [svg](https://docs.rs/svg/index.html)
- SVG 1.1 backend. Renders a `Drawing`
- [token](https://docs.rs/token/index.html)
- Token set for the pic language, mirroring dpic’s `dpic.toks`.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Math](https://docs.rs/struct.MathSpan.html)- Span
- A typeset math label: a self-contained SVG fragment (glyph paths only, rasterizable with no font database) plus exact metrics in inches.

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [CIRCUITS](https://docs.rs/constant.CIRCUITS.html)
- Bundled native circuit-element library (the `define`dialect). Prepend it to source to use`resistor`,`capacitor`, … See`std/circuits.pic`.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [animations_](https://docs.rs/fn.animations_json.html)- json
- Build the JSON animation manifest array (`[{id,effect,start,duration},…]`) for an already-compiled drawing.
- [compile](https://docs.rs/fn.compile.html)
- Compile pic source into a placed-primitive `Drawing`
- [compile_](https://docs.rs/fn.compile_in_dir.html)- in_ - dir
- Compile pic source, resolving `copy "file"`includes relative to`base`.
- [compile_](https://docs.rs/fn.compile_json.html)- json
- Compile to a single JSON object `{ "svg": "...", "animations": [...], "diagnostics": [...] }`, or`{ "error": "..." }`on failure. This is the entry point the WASM wrapper and browser playground consume.
- [diagnostics_](https://docs.rs/fn.diagnostics_json.html)- json
- Build the JSON diagnostic array emitted by pic `print`statements.
- [render_](https://docs.rs/fn.render_svg.html)- svg
- Compile pic source directly to an SVG string.
- [render_](https://docs.rs/fn.render_svg_in_dir.html)- svg_ - in_ - dir
- Render pic source to SVG, resolving `copy "file"`includes relative to`base`.
- [set_](https://docs.rs/fn.set_math_renderer.html)- math_ - renderer
- Register the process-wide math renderer. The first call wins; later calls are ignored (returns whether this call installed the renderer).

# mockforge_vbr - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/mockforge-vbr/0.3.198/mockforge_vbr/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#mockforge-virtual-backend-reality-vbr-engine)MockForge Virtual Backend Reality (VBR) Engine

The VBR engine creates stateful mock servers with persistent virtual databases, auto-generated CRUD APIs, relationship constraints, session management, and time-based data evolution.

[§](https://docs.rs#overview)Overview

VBR acts like a mini real backend with:

- Persistent virtual database (SQLite, JSON, in-memory options)
- CRUD APIs auto-generated from entity schemas
- Relationship modeling and constraint enforcement
- User session & auth emulation
- Time-based data evolution (data aging, expiring sessions)

[§](https://docs.rs#example-usage)Example Usage

```
use mockforge_vbr::{VbrEngine, VbrConfig};
let config = VbrConfig::default()
    .with_storage_backend(mockforge_vbr::StorageBackend::Sqlite {
        path: "./data/vbr.db".into(),
    });
let engine = VbrEngine::new(config).await?;
// Define entities and generate living API
```

# overseerd_app - Rust

## Expand description

The Overseerd protocol-agnostic application core.

This crate ties the DI engine, config, hooks, and dirs into a runnable [ App](https://docs.rs/app/struct.App.html) that is
generic over the

[it installs. It owns the](https://docs.rs/protocol/trait.ProtocolPlugin.html)

`ProtocolPlugin`[, the agnostic](https://docs.rs/app/struct.AppBuilder.html)

`AppBuilder`[, scope planning, the lifecycle/serve envelope, the](https://docs.rs/registry/struct.AppRegistry.html)

`AppRegistry`[handle a protocol drives requests through, and the](https://docs.rs/runtime/struct.AppRuntime.html)

`AppRuntime`[/](https://docs.rs/protocol/trait.Plugin.html)

`Plugin`[/](https://docs.rs/protocol/trait.Protocol.html)

`Protocol`[seam.](https://docs.rs/protocol/trait.Serve.html)

`Serve`It is *protocol-agnostic*: it knows nothing of RPC, HTTP, or any wire format. A protocol
(the native RPC daemon, a future axum binding) is a sibling crate that implements these
traits over this foundation.

# overseerd_axum_macros - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/overseerd-axum-macros/0.9.0/overseerd_axum_macros/

## Expand description

The Overseerd **axum/HTTP controller** macros: `#[controller]`, `#[handlers]`, and the
route attributes (`#[get]`, `#[post]`, `#[put]`, `#[delete]`, `#[patch]`, `#[head]`,
`#[options]`, and the raw `#[route(METHOD, "/path")]`). They emit `::overseerd::web::*`
types, so they live in their own crate rather than the core `overseerd-macros`, built on
the shared [ overseerd_macros_core](https://docs.rs/overseerd-macros-core/0.9.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/overseerd_macros_core/index.html) codegen.

Re-exported through the `overseerd` facade’s `web` module; depend on the facade, not this
crate directly.

- `#[controller]`is a- **router component**: a- `#[component]`(field-injected singleton) plus a controller header, its- `{Controller}Routes`slice, and its- `ControllerDescriptor`.
- `#[handlers]`is- `MethodArgs<AxumHandlers>`— the base impl macro (- `#[methods]`:- `#[init]`- `#[hook]`) plus the route extension, which registers each route-attributed method.

- The route attributes mark a method inside a `#[handlers]`impl (stripped by`#[handlers]`).

## Attribute Macros[§](https://docs.rs#attributes)

- [controller](https://docs.rs/attr.controller.html)
- Declares a **controller**— a router component exposing HTTP routes.
- [delete](https://docs.rs/attr.delete.html)
- Marks a `DELETE`route inside a`#[handlers]`impl (see`get`
- [get](https://docs.rs/attr.get.html)
- Marks a `GET`route inside a`#[handlers]`impl. A marker consumed and stripped by`#[handlers]`; used on its own it emits a`compile_error!`.
- [handlers](https://docs.rs/attr.handlers.html)
- Contributes the route methods (and an optional `#[init]`/`#[hook]`s) of an inherent`impl`block to the controller of`Self`.
- [head](https://docs.rs/attr.head.html)
- Marks a `HEAD`route inside a`#[handlers]`impl (see`get`
- [message](https://docs.rs/attr.message.html)
- Marks a WebSocket message handler inside a `#[handlers]`impl of a`#[controller(ws = ..)]`:`#[message("destination")]`. A marker consumed and stripped by`#[handlers]`; used on its own it emits a`compile_error!`.
- [options](https://docs.rs/attr.options.html)
- Marks an `OPTIONS`route inside a`#[handlers]`impl (see`get`
- [patch](https://docs.rs/attr.patch.html)
- Marks a `PATCH`route inside a`#[handlers]`impl (see`get`
- [post](https://docs.rs/attr.post.html)
- Marks a `POST`route inside a`#[handlers]`impl (see`get`
- [put](https://docs.rs/attr.put.html)
- Marks a `PUT`route inside a`#[handlers]`impl (see`get`
- [route](https://docs.rs/attr.route.html)
- Marks a route by explicit method inside a `#[handlers]`impl:`#[route(METHOD, "/path")]`(see`get`
- [topics](https://docs.rs/attr.topics.html)
- Declares a **STOMP topic set**: an enum whose variants each carry a`#[topic("/topic/..")]`destination and a single payload type. Emits an`impl Topic`(typed server publish) and a`{Enum}Client<C>`with one`subscribe_<variant>()`per topic (typed client subscribe), so the same enum is the single source of truth for both sides. See the crate docs for an example.

# pest 2.8.6 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/pest/2.8.6

# pest. The Elegant Parser

pest is a general purpose parser written in Rust with a focus on accessibility,
correctness, and performance. It uses parsing expression grammars
(or [PEG](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parsing_expression_grammar)) as input, which are similar in spirit to regular expressions, but
which offer the enhanced expressivity needed to parse complex languages.

## Getting started

The recommended way to start parsing with pest is to read the official [book](https://pest.rs/book).

Other helpful resources:

- API reference on [docs.rs](https://docs.rs/pest)
- play with grammars and share them on our [fiddle](https://pest.rs/#editor)
- find previous common questions answered or ask questions on [GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/pest-parser/pest/discussions)
- leave feedback, ask questions, or greet us on [Gitter](https://gitter.im/pest-parser/pest)or[Discord](https://discord.gg/XEGACtWpT2)

## Example

The following is an example of a grammar for a list of alphanumeric identifiers where all identifiers don't start with a digit:

```
alpha =
digit =
ident =
ident_list = _
          // ^
          // ident_list rule is silent which means it produces no tokens
```
Grammars are saved in separate .pest files which are never mixed with procedural code. This results in an always up-to-date formalization of a language that is easy to read and maintain.

## Meaningful error reporting

Based on the grammar definition, the parser also includes automatic error
reporting. For the example above, the input `"123"` will result in:

```
thread 'main' panicked at ' --> 1:1
  |
1 | 123
  | ^---
  |
  = unexpected digit', src/main.rs:12
```
while `"ab *"` will result in:

```
thread 'main' panicked at ' --> 1:1
  |
1 | ab *
  |    ^---
  |
  = expected ident', src/main.rs:12
```
These error messages can be obtained from their default `Display` implementation,
e.g. `panic!("{}", parser_result.unwrap_err())` or `println!("{}", e)`.

## Pairs API

The grammar can be used to derive a `Parser` implementation automatically.
Parsing returns an iterator of nested token pairs:

```
use Parser;
use Parser;
;
```
This produces the following output:

```
Rule:    ident
Span:    Span { start: 0, end: 2 }
Text:    a1
Letter:  a
Digit:   1
Rule:    ident
Span:    Span { start: 3, end: 5 }
Text:    b2
Letter:  b
Digit:   2
```
### Defining multiple parsers in a single file

The current automatic `Parser` derivation will produce the `Rule` enum
which would have name conflicts if one tried to define multiple such structs
that automatically derive `Parser`. One possible way around it is to put each
parser struct in a separate namespace:

```
```
## Other features

- Precedence climbing
- Input handling
- Custom errors
- Runs on stable Rust

## no_std support

The `pest` and `pest_derive` crates can be built without the Rust standard
library and target embedded environments. To do so, you need to disable
their default features. In your `Cargo.toml`, you can specify it as follows:

```
[]
# ...
 = {  = "2",  = false }
 = {  = "2",  = false }
```
If you want to build these crates in the pest repository's workspace, you can
pass the `--no-default-features` flag to `cargo` and specify these crates using
the `--package` (`-p`) flag. For example:

```
```

# pest - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/pest/2.8.6/target-redirect/pest/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#pest-the-elegant-parser)pest. The Elegant Parser

pest is a general purpose parser written in Rust with a focus on accessibility, correctness,
and performance. It uses parsing expression grammars (or [PEG](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parsing_expression_grammar)) as input, which are similar in
spirit to regular expressions, but which offer the enhanced expressivity needed to parse
complex languages.

[§](https://docs.rs#getting-started)Getting started

The recommended way to start parsing with pest is to read the official [book](https://pest.rs/book).

Other helpful resources:

- API reference on [docs.rs](https://docs.rs/pest)
- play with grammars and share them on our [fiddle](https://pest.rs/#editor)
- find previous common questions answered or ask questions on [GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/pest-parser/pest/discussions)
- leave feedback, ask questions, or greet us on [Gitter](https://gitter.im/pest-parser/pest)or[Discord](https://discord.gg/XEGACtWpT2)

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

The core of pest is the trait [ Parser](https://docs.rs/trait.Parser.html), which provides an interface to the parsing
functionality.

The accompanying crate `pest_derive` can automatically generate a [ Parser](https://docs.rs/trait.Parser.html) from a PEG
grammar. Using

`pest_derive` is highly encouraged, but it is also possible to implement
[manually if required.](https://docs.rs/trait.Parser.html)

`Parser`[§](https://docs.rs#pest-files)`.pest` files

Grammar definitions reside in custom `.pest` files located in the crate `src` directory.
Parsers are automatically generated from these files using `#[derive(Parser)]` and a special
`#[grammar = "..."]` attribute on a dummy struct.

The syntax of `.pest` files is documented in the [ pest_derive crate](https://docs.rs/pest_derive/).

[§](https://docs.rs#inline-grammars)Inline grammars

Grammars can also be inlined by using the `#[grammar_inline = "..."]` attribute.

[§](https://docs.rs#grammar)Grammar

A grammar is a series of rules separated by whitespace, possibly containing comments.

[§](https://docs.rs#comments)Comments

Comments start with `//` and end at the end of the line.

`// a comment`[§](https://docs.rs#rules)Rules

Rules have the following form:

The name of the rule is formed from alphanumeric characters or `_` with the condition that the
first character is not a digit and is used to create token pairs. When the rule starts being
parsed, the starting part of the token is being produced, with the ending part being produced
when the rule finishes parsing.

The following token pair notation `a(b(), c())` denotes the tokens: start `a`, start `b`, end
`b`, start `c`, end `c`, end `a`.

[§](https://docs.rs#modifiers)Modifiers

Modifiers are optional and can be one of `_`, `@`, `$`, or `!`. These modifiers change the
behavior of the rules.

-
Silent ( `_`)Silent rules do not create token pairs during parsing, nor are they error-reported. Parsing `"ab"`produces the token pair`b()`.
-
Atomic ( `@`)Atomic rules do not accept whitespace or comments within their expressions and have a cascading effect on any rule they call. I.e. rules that are not atomic but are called by atomic rules behave atomically. Any rules called by atomic rules do not generate token pairs. Parsing `"ab"`produces the token pair`b()`, while`"a b"`produces an error.
-
Compound-atomic ( `$`)Compound-atomic are identical to atomic rules with the exception that rules called by them are not forbidden from generating token pairs. Parsing `"ab"`produces the token pairs`b(a())`, while`"a b"`produces an error.
-
Non-atomic ( `!`)Non-atomic are identical to normal rules with the exception that they stop the cascading effect of atomic and compound-atomic rules. Parsing both `"ab"`and`"a b"`produce the token pairs`c(a())`.

[§](https://docs.rs#expressions)Expressions

Expressions can be either terminals or non-terminals.

- Terminals

| Terminal | Usage |
|---|---|
| `"a"` | matches the exact string `"a"` |
| `^"a"` | matches the exact string `"a"`case insensitively (ASCII only) |
| `'a'..'z'` | matches one character between `'a'`and`'z'` |
| `a` | matches rule `a` |

Strings and characters follow
[Rust’s escape mechanisms](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/tokens.html#byte-escapes), while
identifiers can contain alphanumeric characters and underscores (`_`), as long as they do not
start with a digit.

- Non-terminals

| Non-terminal | Usage |
|---|---|
| `(e)` | matches `e` |
| `e1 ~ e2` | matches the sequence `e1``e2` |
| `e1 | e2` | matches either `e1`or`e2` |
| `e*` | matches `e`zero or more times |
| `e+` | matches `e`one or more times |
| `e{n}` | matches `e`exactly`n`times |
| `e{, n}` | matches `e`at most`n`times |
| `e{n,}` | matches `e`at least`n`times |
| `e{m, n}` | matches `e`between`m`and`n`times inclusively |
| `e?` | optionally matches `e` |
| `&e` | matches `e`without making progress |
| `!e` | matches if `e`doesn’t match without making progress |
| `PUSH(e)` | matches `e`and pushes it’s captured string down the stack |

where `e`, `e1`, and `e2` are expressions.

Matching is greedy, without backtracking. Note the difference in behavior for these two rules in matching identifiers that don’t end in an underscore:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
// input: ab_bb_b
identifier = @{ "a" ~ ("b"|"_")* ~ "b" }
// matches:      a     b_bb_b       nothing -> error!
identifier = @{ "a" ~ ("_"* ~ "b")* }
// matches:      a     b, _bb, _b   in three repetitions
```
Expressions can modify the stack only if they match the input. For example,
if `e1` in the compound expression `e1 | e2` does not match the input, then
it does not modify the stack, so `e2` sees the stack in the same state as
`e1` did. Repetitions and optionals (`e*`, `e+`, `e{, n}`, `e{n,}`,
`e{m,n}`, `e?`) can modify the stack each time `e` matches. The `!e` and `&e`
expressions are a special case; they never modify the stack.
Many languages have “keyword” tokens (e.g. if, for, while) as well as general
tokens (e.g. identifier) that matches any word. In order to match a keyword,
generally, you may need to restrict that is not immediately followed by another
letter or digit (otherwise it would be matched as an identifier).

[§](https://docs.rs#special-rules)Special rules

Special rules can be called within the grammar. They are:

- `WHITESPACE`- runs between rules and sub-rules
- `COMMENT`- runs between rules and sub-rules
- `ANY`- matches exactly one- `char`
- `SOI`- (start-of-input) matches only when a- `Parser`is still at the starting position
- `EOI`- (end-of-input) matches only when a- `Parser`has reached its end
- `PUSH`- matches a string and pushes it to the stack
- `PUSH_LITERAL`- pushes a literal string to the stack
- `POP`- pops a string from the stack and matches it
- `POP_ALL`- pops the entire state of the stack and matches it
- `PEEK`- peeks a string from the stack and matches it
- `PEEK[a..b]`- peeks part of the stack and matches it
- `PEEK_ALL`- peeks the entire state of the stack and matches it
- `DROP`- drops the top of the stack (fails to match if the stack is empty)

`WHITESPACE` and `COMMENT` should be defined manually if needed. All other rules cannot be
overridden.

[§](https://docs.rs#whitespace-and-comment)`WHITESPACE` and `COMMENT`

When defined, these rules get matched automatically in sequences (`~`) and repetitions
(`*`, `+`) between expressions. Atomic rules and those rules called by atomic rules are exempt
from this behavior.

These rules should be defined so as to match one whitespace character and one comment only since they are run in repetitions.

If both `WHITESPACE` and `COMMENT` are defined, this grammar:

is effectively transformed into this one behind the scenes:

[§](https://docs.rs#push-push_literal-pop-drop-and-peek)`PUSH`, `PUSH_LITERAL`, `POP`, `DROP`, and `PEEK`

`PUSH(e)` simply pushes the captured string of the expression `e` down a stack. This stack can
then later be used to match grammar based on its content with `POP` and `PEEK`.

`PUSH_LITERAL("a")` pushes the argument to the stack without considering the input. The
argument must be a literal string. This is often useful in conjunction with another rule before
it. For example, `"[" ~ PUSH_LITERAL("]")` will look for an opening bracket `[` and, if it
finds one, will push a closing bracket `]` to the stack. **Note**: `PUSH_LITERAL` requires the
`grammar-extras` feature to be enabled.

`PEEK` always matches the string at the top of stack. So, if the stack contains `["b", "a"]`
(`"a"` being on top), this grammar:

is effectively transformed into at parse time:

`POP` works the same way with the exception that it pops the string off of the stack if the
match worked. With the stack from above, if `POP` matches `"a"`, the stack will be mutated
to `["b"]`.

`DROP` makes it possible to remove the string at the top of the stack
without matching it. If the stack is nonempty, `DROP` drops the top of the
stack. If the stack is empty, then `DROP` fails to match.

[§](https://docs.rs#advanced-peeking)Advanced peeking

`PEEK[start..end]` and `PEEK_ALL` allow to peek deeper into the stack. The syntax works exactly
like Rust’s exclusive slice syntax. Additionally, negative indices can be used to indicate an
offset from the top. If the end lies before or at the start, the expression matches (as does
a `PEEK_ALL` on an empty stack). With the stack `["c", "b", "a"]` (`"a"` on top):

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
fill = PUSH("c") ~ PUSH("b") ~ PUSH("a")
v = { PEEK_ALL } = { "a" ~ "b" ~ "c" }  // top to bottom
w = { PEEK[..] } = { "c" ~ "b" ~ "a" }  // bottom to top
x = { PEEK[1..2] } = { PEEK[1..-1] } = { "b" }
y = { PEEK[..-2] } = { PEEK[0..1] } = { "a" }
z = { PEEK[1..] } = { PEEK[-2..3] } = { "c" ~ "b" }
n = { PEEK[2..-2] } = { PEEK[2..1] } = { "" }
```
For historical reasons, `PEEK_ALL` matches from top to bottom, while `PEEK[start..end]` matches
from bottom to top. There is currently no syntax to match a slice of the stack top to bottom.

[§](https://docs.rs#rule)`Rule`

All rules defined or used in the grammar populate a generated `enum` called `Rule`. This
implements `pest`’s `RuleType` and can be used throughout the API.

[§](https://docs.rs#built-in-rules)`Built-in rules`

Pest also comes with a number of built-in rules for convenience. They are:

- `ASCII_DIGIT`- matches a numeric character from 0..9
- `ASCII_NONZERO_DIGIT`- matches a numeric character from 1..9
- `ASCII_BIN_DIGIT`- matches a numeric character from 0..1
- `ASCII_OCT_DIGIT`- matches a numeric character from 0..7
- `ASCII_HEX_DIGIT`- matches a numeric character from 0..9 or a..f or A..F
- `ASCII_ALPHA_LOWER`- matches a character from a..z
- `ASCII_ALPHA_UPPER`- matches a character from A..Z
- `ASCII_ALPHA`- matches a character from a..z or A..Z
- `ASCII_ALPHANUMERIC`- matches a character from a..z or A..Z or 0..9
- `ASCII`- matches a character from \x00..\x7f
- `NEWLINE`- matches either “\n” or “\r\n” or “\r”

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [error](https://docs.rs/error/index.html)
- Types for different kinds of parsing failures.
- [iterators](https://docs.rs/iterators/index.html)
- Types and iterators for parser output.
- [pratt_](https://docs.rs/pratt_parser/index.html)- parser
- Constructs useful in prefix, postfix, and infix operator parsing with the Pratt parsing method.
- [prec_](https://docs.rs/prec_climber/index.html)- climber - Deprecated
- Constructs useful in infix operator parsing with the precedence climbing method.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [fails_](https://docs.rs/macro.fails_with.html)- with
- Testing tool that compares produced errors.
- [parses_](https://docs.rs/macro.parses_to.html)- to
- Testing tool that compares produced tokens.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Lines](https://docs.rs/struct.Lines.html)
- Line iterator for Spans, created by `Span::lines()`
- [Lines](https://docs.rs/struct.LinesSpan.html)- Span
- Line iterator for Spans, created by `Span::lines_span()`
- [Parser](https://docs.rs/struct.ParserState.html)- State
- The complete state of a `Parser`
- [Position](https://docs.rs/struct.Position.html)
- A cursor position in a `&str`which provides useful methods to manually parse that string.
- [Span](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html)
- A span over a `&str`. It is created from either[two](https://docs.rs/struct.Position.html#method.span)or from a`Position`s`Pair`
- [Stack](https://docs.rs/struct.Stack.html)
- Implementation of a `Stack`which maintains popped elements and length of previous states in order to rewind the stack to a previous state.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Atomicity](https://docs.rs/enum.Atomicity.html)
- The current atomicity of a `ParserState`
- [Lookahead](https://docs.rs/enum.Lookahead.html)
- The current lookahead status of a `ParserState`
- [Match](https://docs.rs/enum.MatchDir.html)- Dir
- Match direction for the stack. Used in `PEEK[a..b]`/`stack_match_peek_slice`.
- [Token](https://docs.rs/enum.Token.html)
- A token generated by a `Parser`.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Parser](https://docs.rs/trait.Parser.html)
- A trait with a single method that parses strings.
- [Rule](https://docs.rs/trait.RuleType.html)- Type
- A trait which parser rules must implement.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [merge_](https://docs.rs/fn.merge_spans.html)- spans
- Merges two spans into one.
- [set_](https://docs.rs/fn.set_call_limit.html)- call_ - limit
- Sets the maximum call limit for the parser state to prevent stack overflows or excessive execution times in some grammars. If set, the calls are tracked as a running total over all non-terminal rules that can nest closures (which are passed to transform the parser state).
- [set_](https://docs.rs/fn.set_error_detail.html)- error_ - detail
- Sets whether information for more error details should be collected. This is useful for debugging parser errors (as it leads to more comprehensive error messages), but it has a higher performance cost. (hence, it’s off by default)
- [state](https://docs.rs/fn.state.html)
- Creates a `ParserState`from a`&str`, supplying it to a closure`f`.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Parse](https://docs.rs/type.ParseResult.html)- Result
- Type alias to simplify specifying the return value of chained closures.

# pest - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/pest/2.8.6/pest/index.html

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#pest-the-elegant-parser)pest. The Elegant Parser

pest is a general purpose parser written in Rust with a focus on accessibility, correctness,
and performance. It uses parsing expression grammars (or [PEG](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parsing_expression_grammar)) as input, which are similar in
spirit to regular expressions, but which offer the enhanced expressivity needed to parse
complex languages.

[§](https://docs.rs#getting-started)Getting started

The recommended way to start parsing with pest is to read the official [book](https://pest.rs/book).

Other helpful resources:

- API reference on [docs.rs](https://docs.rs/pest)
- play with grammars and share them on our [fiddle](https://pest.rs/#editor)
- find previous common questions answered or ask questions on [GitHub Discussions](https://github.com/pest-parser/pest/discussions)
- leave feedback, ask questions, or greet us on [Gitter](https://gitter.im/pest-parser/pest)or[Discord](https://discord.gg/XEGACtWpT2)

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

The core of pest is the trait [ Parser](https://docs.rs/trait.Parser.html), which provides an interface to the parsing
functionality.

The accompanying crate `pest_derive` can automatically generate a [ Parser](https://docs.rs/trait.Parser.html) from a PEG
grammar. Using

`pest_derive` is highly encouraged, but it is also possible to implement
[manually if required.](https://docs.rs/trait.Parser.html)

`Parser`[§](https://docs.rs#pest-files)`.pest` files

Grammar definitions reside in custom `.pest` files located in the crate `src` directory.
Parsers are automatically generated from these files using `#[derive(Parser)]` and a special
`#[grammar = "..."]` attribute on a dummy struct.

The syntax of `.pest` files is documented in the [ pest_derive crate](https://docs.rs/pest_derive/).

[§](https://docs.rs#inline-grammars)Inline grammars

Grammars can also be inlined by using the `#[grammar_inline = "..."]` attribute.

[§](https://docs.rs#grammar)Grammar

A grammar is a series of rules separated by whitespace, possibly containing comments.

[§](https://docs.rs#comments)Comments

Comments start with `//` and end at the end of the line.

`// a comment`[§](https://docs.rs#rules)Rules

Rules have the following form:

The name of the rule is formed from alphanumeric characters or `_` with the condition that the
first character is not a digit and is used to create token pairs. When the rule starts being
parsed, the starting part of the token is being produced, with the ending part being produced
when the rule finishes parsing.

The following token pair notation `a(b(), c())` denotes the tokens: start `a`, start `b`, end
`b`, start `c`, end `c`, end `a`.

[§](https://docs.rs#modifiers)Modifiers

Modifiers are optional and can be one of `_`, `@`, `$`, or `!`. These modifiers change the
behavior of the rules.

-
Silent ( `_`)Silent rules do not create token pairs during parsing, nor are they error-reported. Parsing `"ab"`produces the token pair`b()`.
-
Atomic ( `@`)Atomic rules do not accept whitespace or comments within their expressions and have a cascading effect on any rule they call. I.e. rules that are not atomic but are called by atomic rules behave atomically. Any rules called by atomic rules do not generate token pairs. Parsing `"ab"`produces the token pair`b()`, while`"a b"`produces an error.
-
Compound-atomic ( `$`)Compound-atomic are identical to atomic rules with the exception that rules called by them are not forbidden from generating token pairs. Parsing `"ab"`produces the token pairs`b(a())`, while`"a b"`produces an error.
-
Non-atomic ( `!`)Non-atomic are identical to normal rules with the exception that they stop the cascading effect of atomic and compound-atomic rules. Parsing both `"ab"`and`"a b"`produce the token pairs`c(a())`.

[§](https://docs.rs#expressions)Expressions

Expressions can be either terminals or non-terminals.

- Terminals

| Terminal | Usage |
|---|---|
| `"a"` | matches the exact string `"a"` |
| `^"a"` | matches the exact string `"a"`case insensitively (ASCII only) |
| `'a'..'z'` | matches one character between `'a'`and`'z'` |
| `a` | matches rule `a` |

Strings and characters follow
[Rust’s escape mechanisms](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/tokens.html#byte-escapes), while
identifiers can contain alphanumeric characters and underscores (`_`), as long as they do not
start with a digit.

- Non-terminals

| Non-terminal | Usage |
|---|---|
| `(e)` | matches `e` |
| `e1 ~ e2` | matches the sequence `e1``e2` |
| `e1 | e2` | matches either `e1`or`e2` |
| `e*` | matches `e`zero or more times |
| `e+` | matches `e`one or more times |
| `e{n}` | matches `e`exactly`n`times |
| `e{, n}` | matches `e`at most`n`times |
| `e{n,}` | matches `e`at least`n`times |
| `e{m, n}` | matches `e`between`m`and`n`times inclusively |
| `e?` | optionally matches `e` |
| `&e` | matches `e`without making progress |
| `!e` | matches if `e`doesn’t match without making progress |
| `PUSH(e)` | matches `e`and pushes it’s captured string down the stack |

where `e`, `e1`, and `e2` are expressions.

Matching is greedy, without backtracking. Note the difference in behavior for these two rules in matching identifiers that don’t end in an underscore:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
// input: ab_bb_b
identifier = @{ "a" ~ ("b"|"_")* ~ "b" }
// matches:      a     b_bb_b       nothing -> error!
identifier = @{ "a" ~ ("_"* ~ "b")* }
// matches:      a     b, _bb, _b   in three repetitions
```
Expressions can modify the stack only if they match the input. For example,
if `e1` in the compound expression `e1 | e2` does not match the input, then
it does not modify the stack, so `e2` sees the stack in the same state as
`e1` did. Repetitions and optionals (`e*`, `e+`, `e{, n}`, `e{n,}`,
`e{m,n}`, `e?`) can modify the stack each time `e` matches. The `!e` and `&e`
expressions are a special case; they never modify the stack.
Many languages have “keyword” tokens (e.g. if, for, while) as well as general
tokens (e.g. identifier) that matches any word. In order to match a keyword,
generally, you may need to restrict that is not immediately followed by another
letter or digit (otherwise it would be matched as an identifier).

[§](https://docs.rs#special-rules)Special rules

Special rules can be called within the grammar. They are:

- `WHITESPACE`- runs between rules and sub-rules
- `COMMENT`- runs between rules and sub-rules
- `ANY`- matches exactly one- `char`
- `SOI`- (start-of-input) matches only when a- `Parser`is still at the starting position
- `EOI`- (end-of-input) matches only when a- `Parser`has reached its end
- `PUSH`- matches a string and pushes it to the stack
- `PUSH_LITERAL`- pushes a literal string to the stack
- `POP`- pops a string from the stack and matches it
- `POP_ALL`- pops the entire state of the stack and matches it
- `PEEK`- peeks a string from the stack and matches it
- `PEEK[a..b]`- peeks part of the stack and matches it
- `PEEK_ALL`- peeks the entire state of the stack and matches it
- `DROP`- drops the top of the stack (fails to match if the stack is empty)

`WHITESPACE` and `COMMENT` should be defined manually if needed. All other rules cannot be
overridden.

[§](https://docs.rs#whitespace-and-comment)`WHITESPACE` and `COMMENT`

When defined, these rules get matched automatically in sequences (`~`) and repetitions
(`*`, `+`) between expressions. Atomic rules and those rules called by atomic rules are exempt
from this behavior.

These rules should be defined so as to match one whitespace character and one comment only since they are run in repetitions.

If both `WHITESPACE` and `COMMENT` are defined, this grammar:

is effectively transformed into this one behind the scenes:

[§](https://docs.rs#push-push_literal-pop-drop-and-peek)`PUSH`, `PUSH_LITERAL`, `POP`, `DROP`, and `PEEK`

`PUSH(e)` simply pushes the captured string of the expression `e` down a stack. This stack can
then later be used to match grammar based on its content with `POP` and `PEEK`.

`PUSH_LITERAL("a")` pushes the argument to the stack without considering the input. The
argument must be a literal string. This is often useful in conjunction with another rule before
it. For example, `"[" ~ PUSH_LITERAL("]")` will look for an opening bracket `[` and, if it
finds one, will push a closing bracket `]` to the stack. **Note**: `PUSH_LITERAL` requires the
`grammar-extras` feature to be enabled.

`PEEK` always matches the string at the top of stack. So, if the stack contains `["b", "a"]`
(`"a"` being on top), this grammar:

is effectively transformed into at parse time:

`POP` works the same way with the exception that it pops the string off of the stack if the
match worked. With the stack from above, if `POP` matches `"a"`, the stack will be mutated
to `["b"]`.

`DROP` makes it possible to remove the string at the top of the stack
without matching it. If the stack is nonempty, `DROP` drops the top of the
stack. If the stack is empty, then `DROP` fails to match.

[§](https://docs.rs#advanced-peeking)Advanced peeking

`PEEK[start..end]` and `PEEK_ALL` allow to peek deeper into the stack. The syntax works exactly
like Rust’s exclusive slice syntax. Additionally, negative indices can be used to indicate an
offset from the top. If the end lies before or at the start, the expression matches (as does
a `PEEK_ALL` on an empty stack). With the stack `["c", "b", "a"]` (`"a"` on top):

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
fill = PUSH("c") ~ PUSH("b") ~ PUSH("a")
v = { PEEK_ALL } = { "a" ~ "b" ~ "c" }  // top to bottom
w = { PEEK[..] } = { "c" ~ "b" ~ "a" }  // bottom to top
x = { PEEK[1..2] } = { PEEK[1..-1] } = { "b" }
y = { PEEK[..-2] } = { PEEK[0..1] } = { "a" }
z = { PEEK[1..] } = { PEEK[-2..3] } = { "c" ~ "b" }
n = { PEEK[2..-2] } = { PEEK[2..1] } = { "" }
```
For historical reasons, `PEEK_ALL` matches from top to bottom, while `PEEK[start..end]` matches
from bottom to top. There is currently no syntax to match a slice of the stack top to bottom.

[§](https://docs.rs#rule)`Rule`

All rules defined or used in the grammar populate a generated `enum` called `Rule`. This
implements `pest`’s `RuleType` and can be used throughout the API.

[§](https://docs.rs#built-in-rules)`Built-in rules`

Pest also comes with a number of built-in rules for convenience. They are:

- `ASCII_DIGIT`- matches a numeric character from 0..9
- `ASCII_NONZERO_DIGIT`- matches a numeric character from 1..9
- `ASCII_BIN_DIGIT`- matches a numeric character from 0..1
- `ASCII_OCT_DIGIT`- matches a numeric character from 0..7
- `ASCII_HEX_DIGIT`- matches a numeric character from 0..9 or a..f or A..F
- `ASCII_ALPHA_LOWER`- matches a character from a..z
- `ASCII_ALPHA_UPPER`- matches a character from A..Z
- `ASCII_ALPHA`- matches a character from a..z or A..Z
- `ASCII_ALPHANUMERIC`- matches a character from a..z or A..Z or 0..9
- `ASCII`- matches a character from \x00..\x7f
- `NEWLINE`- matches either “\n” or “\r\n” or “\r”

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [error](https://docs.rs/error/index.html)
- Types for different kinds of parsing failures.
- [iterators](https://docs.rs/iterators/index.html)
- Types and iterators for parser output.
- [pratt_](https://docs.rs/pratt_parser/index.html)- parser
- Constructs useful in prefix, postfix, and infix operator parsing with the Pratt parsing method.
- [prec_](https://docs.rs/prec_climber/index.html)- climber - Deprecated
- Constructs useful in infix operator parsing with the precedence climbing method.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [fails_](https://docs.rs/macro.fails_with.html)- with
- Testing tool that compares produced errors.
- [parses_](https://docs.rs/macro.parses_to.html)- to
- Testing tool that compares produced tokens.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Lines](https://docs.rs/struct.Lines.html)
- Line iterator for Spans, created by `Span::lines()`
- [Lines](https://docs.rs/struct.LinesSpan.html)- Span
- Line iterator for Spans, created by `Span::lines_span()`
- [Parser](https://docs.rs/struct.ParserState.html)- State
- The complete state of a `Parser`
- [Position](https://docs.rs/struct.Position.html)
- A cursor position in a `&str`which provides useful methods to manually parse that string.
- [Span](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html)
- A span over a `&str`. It is created from either[two](https://docs.rs/struct.Position.html#method.span)or from a`Position`s`Pair`
- [Stack](https://docs.rs/struct.Stack.html)
- Implementation of a `Stack`which maintains popped elements and length of previous states in order to rewind the stack to a previous state.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Atomicity](https://docs.rs/enum.Atomicity.html)
- The current atomicity of a `ParserState`
- [Lookahead](https://docs.rs/enum.Lookahead.html)
- The current lookahead status of a `ParserState`
- [Match](https://docs.rs/enum.MatchDir.html)- Dir
- Match direction for the stack. Used in `PEEK[a..b]`/`stack_match_peek_slice`.
- [Token](https://docs.rs/enum.Token.html)
- A token generated by a `Parser`.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Parser](https://docs.rs/trait.Parser.html)
- A trait with a single method that parses strings.
- [Rule](https://docs.rs/trait.RuleType.html)- Type
- A trait which parser rules must implement.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [merge_](https://docs.rs/fn.merge_spans.html)- spans
- Merges two spans into one.
- [set_](https://docs.rs/fn.set_call_limit.html)- call_ - limit
- Sets the maximum call limit for the parser state to prevent stack overflows or excessive execution times in some grammars. If set, the calls are tracked as a running total over all non-terminal rules that can nest closures (which are passed to transform the parser state).
- [set_](https://docs.rs/fn.set_error_detail.html)- error_ - detail
- Sets whether information for more error details should be collected. This is useful for debugging parser errors (as it leads to more comprehensive error messages), but it has a higher performance cost. (hence, it’s off by default)
- [state](https://docs.rs/fn.state.html)
- Creates a `ParserState`from a`&str`, supplying it to a closure`f`.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Parse](https://docs.rs/type.ParseResult.html)- Result
- Type alias to simplify specifying the return value of chained closures.

[15](https://docs.rs#15)//! # pest. The Elegant Parser
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//!
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//! pest is a general purpose parser written in Rust with a focus on accessibility, correctness,
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//! and performance. It uses parsing expression grammars (or [PEG]) as input, which are similar in
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//! spirit to regular expressions, but which offer the enhanced expressivity needed to parse
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//! complex languages.
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//!

[43](https://docs.rs#43)//!
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//! The core of pest is the trait [`Parser`], which provides an interface to the parsing
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//! functionality.
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//!
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//! The accompanying crate `pest_derive` can automatically generate a [`Parser`] from a PEG
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//! grammar. Using `pest_derive` is highly encouraged, but it is also possible to implement
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//! [`Parser`] manually if required.
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//!
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//! ## `.pest` files
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//!
[53](https://docs.rs#53)//! Grammar definitions reside in custom `.pest` files located in the crate `src` directory.
[54](https://docs.rs#54)//! Parsers are automatically generated from these files using `#[derive(Parser)]` and a special
[55](https://docs.rs#55)//! `#[grammar = "..."]` attribute on a dummy struct.
[56](https://docs.rs#56)//!
[57](https://docs.rs#57)//! ```ignore
[58](https://docs.rs#58)//! #[derive(Parser)]
[59](https://docs.rs#59)//! #[grammar = "path/to/my_grammar.pest"] // relative to src
[60](https://docs.rs#60)//! struct MyParser;
[61](https://docs.rs#61)//! ```
[62](https://docs.rs#62)//!
[63](https://docs.rs#63)//! The syntax of `.pest` files is documented in the [`pest_derive` crate].
[64](https://docs.rs#64)//!
[65](https://docs.rs#65)//! ## Inline grammars
[66](https://docs.rs#66)//!
[67](https://docs.rs#67)//! Grammars can also be inlined by using the `#[grammar_inline = "..."]` attribute.
[68](https://docs.rs#68)//!
[69](https://docs.rs#69)//! [`Parser`]: trait.Parser.html
[70](https://docs.rs#70)//! [`pest_derive` crate]: https://docs.rs/pest_derive/
[71](https://docs.rs#71)//!
[72](https://docs.rs#72)//! ## Grammar
[73](https://docs.rs#73)//!
[74](https://docs.rs#74)//! A grammar is a series of rules separated by whitespace, possibly containing comments.
[75](https://docs.rs#75)//!
[76](https://docs.rs#76)//! ### Comments
[77](https://docs.rs#77)//!
[78](https://docs.rs#78)//! Comments start with `//` and end at the end of the line.
[79](https://docs.rs#79)//!
[80](https://docs.rs#80)//! ```text
[81](https://docs.rs#81)//! // a comment
[82](https://docs.rs#82)//! ```
[83](https://docs.rs#83)//!
[84](https://docs.rs#84)//! ### Rules
[85](https://docs.rs#85)//!
[86](https://docs.rs#86)//! Rules have the following form:
[87](https://docs.rs#87)//!
[88](https://docs.rs#88)//! ```ignore
[89](https://docs.rs#89)//! name = optional_modifier { expression }
[90](https://docs.rs#90)//! ```
[91](https://docs.rs#91)//!
[92](https://docs.rs#92)//! The name of the rule is formed from alphanumeric characters or `_` with the condition that the
[93](https://docs.rs#93)//! first character is not a digit and is used to create token pairs. When the rule starts being
[94](https://docs.rs#94)//! parsed, the starting part of the token is being produced, with the ending part being produced
[95](https://docs.rs#95)//! when the rule finishes parsing.
[96](https://docs.rs#96)//!
[97](https://docs.rs#97)//! The following token pair notation `a(b(), c())` denotes the tokens: start `a`, start `b`, end
[98](https://docs.rs#98)//! `b`, start `c`, end `c`, end `a`.
[99](https://docs.rs#99)//!
[100](https://docs.rs#100)//! #### Modifiers
[101](https://docs.rs#101)//!
[102](https://docs.rs#102)//! Modifiers are optional and can be one of `_`, `@`, `$`, or `!`. These modifiers change the
[103](https://docs.rs#103)//! behavior of the rules.
[104](https://docs.rs#104)//!
[105](https://docs.rs#105)//! 1. Silent (`_`)
[106](https://docs.rs#106)//!
[107](https://docs.rs#107)//!     Silent rules do not create token pairs during parsing, nor are they error-reported.
[108](https://docs.rs#108)//!
[109](https://docs.rs#109)//!     ```ignore
[110](https://docs.rs#110)//!     a = _{ "a" }
[111](https://docs.rs#111)//!     b =  { a ~ "b" }
[112](https://docs.rs#112)//!     ```
[113](https://docs.rs#113)//!
[114](https://docs.rs#114)//!     Parsing `"ab"` produces the token pair `b()`.
[115](https://docs.rs#115)//!
[116](https://docs.rs#116)//! 2. Atomic (`@`)
[117](https://docs.rs#117)//!
[118](https://docs.rs#118)//!     Atomic rules do not accept whitespace or comments within their expressions and have a
[119](https://docs.rs#119)//!     cascading effect on any rule they call. I.e. rules that are not atomic but are called by atomic
[120](https://docs.rs#120)//!     rules behave atomically.
[121](https://docs.rs#121)//!
[122](https://docs.rs#122)//!     Any rules called by atomic rules do not generate token pairs.
[123](https://docs.rs#123)//!
[124](https://docs.rs#124)//!     ```ignore
[125](https://docs.rs#125)//!     a =  { "a" }
[126](https://docs.rs#126)//!     b = @{ a ~ "b" }
[127](https://docs.rs#127)//!
[128](https://docs.rs#128)//!     WHITESPACE = _{ " " }
[129](https://docs.rs#129)//!     ```
[130](https://docs.rs#130)//!
[131](https://docs.rs#131)//!     Parsing `"ab"` produces the token pair `b()`, while `"a   b"` produces an error.
[132](https://docs.rs#132)//!
[133](https://docs.rs#133)//! 3. Compound-atomic (`$`)
[134](https://docs.rs#134)//!
[135](https://docs.rs#135)//!     Compound-atomic are identical to atomic rules with the exception that rules called by them are
[136](https://docs.rs#136)//!     not forbidden from generating token pairs.
[137](https://docs.rs#137)//!
[138](https://docs.rs#138)//!     ```ignore
[139](https://docs.rs#139)//!     a =  { "a" }
[140](https://docs.rs#140)//!     b = ${ a ~ "b" }
[141](https://docs.rs#141)//!
[142](https://docs.rs#142)//!     WHITESPACE = _{ " " }
[143](https://docs.rs#143)//!     ```
[144](https://docs.rs#144)//!
[145](https://docs.rs#145)//!     Parsing `"ab"` produces the token pairs `b(a())`, while `"a   b"` produces an error.
[146](https://docs.rs#146)//!
[147](https://docs.rs#147)//! 4. Non-atomic (`!`)
[148](https://docs.rs#148)//!
[149](https://docs.rs#149)//!     Non-atomic are identical to normal rules with the exception that they stop the cascading effect
[150](https://docs.rs#150)//!     of atomic and compound-atomic rules.
[151](https://docs.rs#151)//!
[152](https://docs.rs#152)//!     ```ignore
[153](https://docs.rs#153)//!     a =  { "a" }
[154](https://docs.rs#154)//!     b = !{ a ~ "b" }
[155](https://docs.rs#155)//!     c = @{ b }
[156](https://docs.rs#156)//!
[157](https://docs.rs#157)//!     WHITESPACE = _{ " " }
[158](https://docs.rs#158)//!     ```
[159](https://docs.rs#159)//!
[160](https://docs.rs#160)//!     Parsing both `"ab"` and `"a   b"` produce the token pairs `c(a())`.
[161](https://docs.rs#161)//!
[162](https://docs.rs#162)//! #### Expressions
[163](https://docs.rs#163)//!
[164](https://docs.rs#164)//! Expressions can be either terminals or non-terminals.
[165](https://docs.rs#165)//!
[166](https://docs.rs#166)//! 1. Terminals
[167](https://docs.rs#167)//!
[168](https://docs.rs#168)//! | Terminal   | Usage                                                          |
[169](https://docs.rs#169)//! |------------|----------------------------------------------------------------|
[170](https://docs.rs#170)//! | `"a"`      | matches the exact string `"a"`                                 |
[171](https://docs.rs#171)//! | `^"a"`     | matches the exact string `"a"` case insensitively (ASCII only) |
[172](https://docs.rs#172)//! | `'a'..'z'` | matches one character between `'a'` and `'z'`                  |
[173](https://docs.rs#173)//! | `a`        | matches rule `a`                                               |
[174](https://docs.rs#174)//!
[175](https://docs.rs#175)//! Strings and characters follow
[176](https://docs.rs#176)//! [Rust's escape mechanisms](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/tokens.html#byte-escapes), while
[177](https://docs.rs#177)//! identifiers can contain alphanumeric characters and underscores (`_`), as long as they do not
[178](https://docs.rs#178)//! start with a digit.
[179](https://docs.rs#179)//!
[180](https://docs.rs#180)//! 2. Non-terminals
[181](https://docs.rs#181)//!
[182](https://docs.rs#182)//! | Non-terminal          | Usage                                                      |
[183](https://docs.rs#183)//! |-----------------------|------------------------------------------------------------|
[184](https://docs.rs#184)//! | `(e)`                 | matches `e`                                                |
[185](https://docs.rs#185)//! | `e1 ~ e2`             | matches the sequence `e1` `e2`                             |
[186](https://docs.rs#186)//! | <code>e1 \| e2</code> | matches either `e1` or `e2`                                |
[187](https://docs.rs#187)//! | `e*`                  | matches `e` zero or more times                             |
[188](https://docs.rs#188)//! | `e+`                  | matches `e` one or more times                              |
[189](https://docs.rs#189)//! | `e{n}`                | matches `e` exactly `n` times                              |
[190](https://docs.rs#190)//! | `e{, n}`              | matches `e` at most `n` times                              |
[191](https://docs.rs#191)//! | `e{n,}`               | matches `e` at least `n` times                             |
[192](https://docs.rs#192)//! | `e{m, n}`             | matches `e` between `m` and `n` times inclusively          |
[193](https://docs.rs#193)//! | `e?`                  | optionally matches `e`                                     |
[194](https://docs.rs#194)//! | `&e`                  | matches `e` without making progress                        |
[195](https://docs.rs#195)//! | `!e`                  | matches if `e` doesn't match without making progress       |
[196](https://docs.rs#196)//! | `PUSH(e)`             | matches `e` and pushes it's captured string down the stack |
[197](https://docs.rs#197)//!
[198](https://docs.rs#198)//! where `e`, `e1`, and `e2` are expressions.
[199](https://docs.rs#199)//!
[200](https://docs.rs#200)//! Matching is greedy, without backtracking.  Note the difference in behavior for
[201](https://docs.rs#201)//! these two rules in matching identifiers that don't end in an underscore:
[202](https://docs.rs#202)//!
[203](https://docs.rs#203)//! ```ignore
[204](https://docs.rs#204)//! // input: ab_bb_b
[205](https://docs.rs#205)//!
[206](https://docs.rs#206)//! identifier = @{ "a" ~ ("b"|"_")* ~ "b" }
[207](https://docs.rs#207)//! // matches:      a     b_bb_b       nothing -> error!
[208](https://docs.rs#208)//!
[209](https://docs.rs#209)//! identifier = @{ "a" ~ ("_"* ~ "b")* }
[210](https://docs.rs#210)//! // matches:      a     b, _bb, _b   in three repetitions
[211](https://docs.rs#211)//! ```
[212](https://docs.rs#212)//!
[213](https://docs.rs#213)//! Expressions can modify the stack only if they match the input. For example,
[214](https://docs.rs#214)//! if `e1` in the compound expression `e1 | e2` does not match the input, then
[215](https://docs.rs#215)//! it does not modify the stack, so `e2` sees the stack in the same state as
[216](https://docs.rs#216)//! `e1` did. Repetitions and optionals (`e*`, `e+`, `e{, n}`, `e{n,}`,
[217](https://docs.rs#217)//! `e{m,n}`, `e?`) can modify the stack each time `e` matches. The `!e` and `&e`
[218](https://docs.rs#218)//! expressions are a special case; they never modify the stack.
[219](https://docs.rs#219)//! Many languages have "keyword" tokens (e.g. if, for, while) as well as general
[220](https://docs.rs#220)//! tokens (e.g. identifier) that matches any word. In order to match a keyword,
[221](https://docs.rs#221)//! generally, you may need to restrict that is not immediately followed by another
[222](https://docs.rs#222)//! letter or digit (otherwise it would be matched as an identifier).
[223](https://docs.rs#223)//!
[224](https://docs.rs#224)//! ## Special rules
[225](https://docs.rs#225)//!
[226](https://docs.rs#226)//! Special rules can be called within the grammar. They are:
[227](https://docs.rs#227)//!
[228](https://docs.rs#228)//! * `WHITESPACE` - runs between rules and sub-rules
[229](https://docs.rs#229)//! * `COMMENT` - runs between rules and sub-rules
[230](https://docs.rs#230)//! * `ANY` - matches exactly one `char`
[231](https://docs.rs#231)//! * `SOI` - (start-of-input) matches only when a `Parser` is still at the starting position
[232](https://docs.rs#232)//! * `EOI` - (end-of-input) matches only when a `Parser` has reached its end
[233](https://docs.rs#233)//! * `PUSH` - matches a string and pushes it to the stack
[234](https://docs.rs#234)//! * `PUSH_LITERAL` - pushes a literal string to the stack
[235](https://docs.rs#235)//! * `POP` - pops a string from the stack and matches it
[236](https://docs.rs#236)//! * `POP_ALL` - pops the entire state of the stack and matches it
[237](https://docs.rs#237)//! * `PEEK` - peeks a string from the stack and matches it
[238](https://docs.rs#238)//! * `PEEK[a..b]` - peeks part of the stack and matches it
[239](https://docs.rs#239)//! * `PEEK_ALL` - peeks the entire state of the stack and matches it
[240](https://docs.rs#240)//! * `DROP` - drops the top of the stack (fails to match if the stack is empty)
[241](https://docs.rs#241)//!
[242](https://docs.rs#242)//! `WHITESPACE` and `COMMENT` should be defined manually if needed. All other rules cannot be
[243](https://docs.rs#243)//! overridden.
[244](https://docs.rs#244)//!
[245](https://docs.rs#245)//! ## `WHITESPACE` and `COMMENT`
[246](https://docs.rs#246)//!
[247](https://docs.rs#247)//! When defined, these rules get matched automatically in sequences (`~`) and repetitions
[248](https://docs.rs#248)//! (`*`, `+`) between expressions. Atomic rules and those rules called by atomic rules are exempt
[249](https://docs.rs#249)//! from this behavior.
[250](https://docs.rs#250)//!
[251](https://docs.rs#251)//! These rules should be defined so as to match one whitespace character and one comment only since
[252](https://docs.rs#252)//! they are run in repetitions.
[253](https://docs.rs#253)//!
[254](https://docs.rs#254)//! If both `WHITESPACE` and `COMMENT` are defined, this grammar:
[255](https://docs.rs#255)//!
[256](https://docs.rs#256)//! ```ignore
[257](https://docs.rs#257)//! a = { b ~ c }
[258](https://docs.rs#258)//! ```
[259](https://docs.rs#259)//!
[260](https://docs.rs#260)//! is effectively transformed into this one behind the scenes:
[261](https://docs.rs#261)//!
[262](https://docs.rs#262)//! ```ignore
[263](https://docs.rs#263)//! a = { b ~ WHITESPACE* ~ (COMMENT ~ WHITESPACE*)* ~ c }
[264](https://docs.rs#264)//! ```
[265](https://docs.rs#265)//!
[266](https://docs.rs#266)//! ## `PUSH`, `PUSH_LITERAL`, `POP`, `DROP`, and `PEEK`
[267](https://docs.rs#267)//!
[268](https://docs.rs#268)//! `PUSH(e)` simply pushes the captured string of the expression `e` down a stack. This stack can
[269](https://docs.rs#269)//! then later be used to match grammar based on its content with `POP` and `PEEK`.
[270](https://docs.rs#270)//!
[271](https://docs.rs#271)//! `PUSH_LITERAL("a")` pushes the argument to the stack without considering the input. The
[272](https://docs.rs#272)//! argument must be a literal string. This is often useful in conjunction with another rule before
[273](https://docs.rs#273)//! it. For example, `"[" ~ PUSH_LITERAL("]")` will look for an opening bracket `[` and, if it
[274](https://docs.rs#274)//! finds one, will push a closing bracket `]` to the stack. **Note**: `PUSH_LITERAL` requires the
[275](https://docs.rs#275)//! `grammar-extras` feature to be enabled.
[276](https://docs.rs#276)//!
[277](https://docs.rs#277)//! `PEEK` always matches the string at the top of stack. So, if the stack contains `["b", "a"]`
[278](https://docs.rs#278)//! (`"a"` being on top), this grammar:
[279](https://docs.rs#279)//!
[280](https://docs.rs#280)//! ```ignore
[281](https://docs.rs#281)//! a = { PEEK }
[282](https://docs.rs#282)//! ```
[283](https://docs.rs#283)//!
[284](https://docs.rs#284)//! is effectively transformed into at parse time:
[285](https://docs.rs#285)//!
[286](https://docs.rs#286)//! ```ignore
[287](https://docs.rs#287)//! a = { "a" }
[288](https://docs.rs#288)//! ```
[289](https://docs.rs#289)//!
[290](https://docs.rs#290)//! `POP` works the same way with the exception that it pops the string off of the stack if the
[291](https://docs.rs#291)//! match worked. With the stack from above, if `POP` matches `"a"`, the stack will be mutated
[292](https://docs.rs#292)//! to `["b"]`.
[293](https://docs.rs#293)//!
[294](https://docs.rs#294)//! `DROP` makes it possible to remove the string at the top of the stack
[295](https://docs.rs#295)//! without matching it. If the stack is nonempty, `DROP` drops the top of the
[296](https://docs.rs#296)//! stack. If the stack is empty, then `DROP` fails to match.
[297](https://docs.rs#297)//!
[298](https://docs.rs#298)//! ### Advanced peeking
[299](https://docs.rs#299)//!
[300](https://docs.rs#300)//! `PEEK[start..end]` and `PEEK_ALL` allow to peek deeper into the stack. The syntax works exactly
[301](https://docs.rs#301)//! like Rust’s exclusive slice syntax. Additionally, negative indices can be used to indicate an
[302](https://docs.rs#302)//! offset from the top. If the end lies before or at the start, the expression matches (as does
[303](https://docs.rs#303)//! a `PEEK_ALL` on an empty stack). With the stack `["c", "b", "a"]` (`"a"` on top):
[304](https://docs.rs#304)//!
[305](https://docs.rs#305)//! ```ignore
[306](https://docs.rs#306)//! fill = PUSH("c") ~ PUSH("b") ~ PUSH("a")
[307](https://docs.rs#307)//! v = { PEEK_ALL } = { "a" ~ "b" ~ "c" }  // top to bottom
[308](https://docs.rs#308)//! w = { PEEK[..] } = { "c" ~ "b" ~ "a" }  // bottom to top
[309](https://docs.rs#309)//! x = { PEEK[1..2] } = { PEEK[1..-1] } = { "b" }
[310](https://docs.rs#310)//! y = { PEEK[..-2] } = { PEEK[0..1] } = { "a" }
[311](https://docs.rs#311)//! z = { PEEK[1..] } = { PEEK[-2..3] } = { "c" ~ "b" }
[312](https://docs.rs#312)//! n = { PEEK[2..-2] } = { PEEK[2..1] } = { "" }
[313](https://docs.rs#313)//! ```
[314](https://docs.rs#314)//!
[315](https://docs.rs#315)//! For historical reasons, `PEEK_ALL` matches from top to bottom, while `PEEK[start..end]` matches
[316](https://docs.rs#316)//! from bottom to top. There is currently no syntax to match a slice of the stack top to bottom.
[317](https://docs.rs#317)//!
[318](https://docs.rs#318)//! ## `Rule`
[319](https://docs.rs#319)//!
[320](https://docs.rs#320)//! All rules defined or used in the grammar populate a generated `enum` called `Rule`. This
[321](https://docs.rs#321)//! implements `pest`'s `RuleType` and can be used throughout the API.
[322](https://docs.rs#322)//!
[323](https://docs.rs#323)//! ## `Built-in rules`
[324](https://docs.rs#324)//!
[325](https://docs.rs#325)//! Pest also comes with a number of built-in rules for convenience. They are:
[326](https://docs.rs#326)//!
[327](https://docs.rs#327)//! * `ASCII_DIGIT` - matches a numeric character from 0..9
[328](https://docs.rs#328)//! * `ASCII_NONZERO_DIGIT` - matches a numeric character from 1..9
[329](https://docs.rs#329)//! * `ASCII_BIN_DIGIT` - matches a numeric character from 0..1
[330](https://docs.rs#330)//! * `ASCII_OCT_DIGIT` - matches a numeric character from 0..7
[331](https://docs.rs#331)//! * `ASCII_HEX_DIGIT` - matches a numeric character from 0..9 or a..f or A..F
[332](https://docs.rs#332)//! * `ASCII_ALPHA_LOWER` - matches a character from a..z
[333](https://docs.rs#333)//! * `ASCII_ALPHA_UPPER` - matches a character from A..Z
[334](https://docs.rs#334)//! * `ASCII_ALPHA` - matches a character from a..z or A..Z
[335](https://docs.rs#335)//! * `ASCII_ALPHANUMERIC` - matches a character from a..z or A..Z or 0..9
[336](https://docs.rs#336)//! * `ASCII` - matches a character from \x00..\x7f
[337](https://docs.rs#337)//! * `NEWLINE` - matches either "\n" or "\r\n" or "\r"
[338](https://docs.rs#338)
[339](https://docs.rs#339)#![doc(html_root_url = "https://docs.rs/pest")]
[340](https://docs.rs#340)
